questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting the hormones made by the anterior pituitary, the pars intermedia and the hypothalamic neurons whose hormones are stored in the posterior pituitary
questions.question: Consider this list: GH, prolactin, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, MSH, oxytocin, vasopressin (ADH), GnRH. How many are synthesised and secreted by the pars distalis (anterior pituitary), and how many are made by hypothalamic neurons but released from the neurohypophysis?
options: A) 8 and 2
B) 7 and 3
C) 4 and 2
D) 6 and 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6 from the pars distalis; 2 (oxytocin, vasopressin) released from the neurohypophysis.
Concept: The pituitary gland is located in a bony cavity called sella turcica and is attached to the hypothalamus by a stalk. It is divided anatomically into an adenohypophysis and a neurohypophysis. The adenohypophysis consists of two portions, pars distalis and pars intermedia; the pars distalis region, commonly called the anterior pituitary, produces growth hormone (GH), prolactin (PRL), thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle stimulating hormone (FSH). The pars intermedia secretes only one hormone, melanocyte stimulating hormone (MSH); in humans it is almost merged with the pars distalis. The neurohypophysis (pars nervosa), also known as the posterior pituitary, stores and releases two hormones, oxytocin and vasopressin, which are actually synthesised by the hypothalamus and transported axonally to the neurohypophysis. The hypothalamus contains groups of neurosecretory cells that produce releasing hormones (e.g. gonadotrophin releasing hormone, GnRH) and inhibiting hormones (e.g. somatostatin), which reach the pituitary through a portal circulatory system and regulate the functions of the anterior pituitary.
Given: Ten hormones listed.
Formula/Principle: Classify each hormone by its site of synthesis and site of release.
Step 1: Pars distalis: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH ⇒ 6.
Step 2: Made in hypothalamus, released from neurohypophysis: oxytocin, vasopressin ⇒ 2.
Step 3: Remaining: MSH (pars intermedia) and GnRH (hypothalamic releasing hormone) ⇒ 6 + 2 + 2 = 10 ✓.
Why: The neurohypophysis is nervous tissue that only stores and releases hormones made by hypothalamic neurons, while the adenohypophysis is glandular tissue that makes its own hormones under hypothalamic control.
Why not the others: (A) Counts MSH and GnRH as anterior pituitary products. (B) Miscounts the posterior lobe. (C) Omits several tropic hormones.
Key point: Anterior pituitary: GH, PRL, TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH; posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH made in the hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The sequence of events from sporogenous tissue to a mature pollen grain, the layers of the pollen wall, and the two cells of the pollen grain at shedding
questions.question: Which sequence and description of microsporogenesis and the male gametophyte is correct?
options: A) Sporogenous tissue → microspore mother cells (2n) → meiosis → microspore tetrads → separated microspores → pollen grains; the pollen wall has a hard exine of sporopollenin, absent at the germ pores, and a thin intine of cellulose and pectin; the mature pollen has a large vegetative cell with abundant food and a small spindle-shaped generative cell, and in over 60 per cent of angiosperms it is shed at this 2-celled stage, the generative cell dividing later into two male gametes
B) Microspore tetrads form by mitosis of the microspore mother cells, so pollen grains are diploid
C) The exine is made of cellulose and the intine of sporopollenin
D) The generative cell is large and stores food, while the vegetative cell divides to form the male gametes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Sporogenous tissue → MMC → meiosis → tetrad → pollen; exine of sporopollenin (with germ pores), intine of cellulose and pectin; vegetative and generative cells.
Concept: When the anther is young, a group of compactly arranged homogenous cells called the sporogenous tissue occupies the centre of each microsporangium. As the anther develops, the cells of the sporogenous tissue undergo meiotic divisions to form microspore tetrads; each cell of the sporogenous tissue is capable of giving rise to a microspore tetrad and is a potential pollen or microspore mother cell. The process of formation of microspores from a pollen mother cell through meiosis is called microsporogenesis. As the anthers mature and dehydrate, the microspores dissociate from each other and develop into pollen grains. The hard outer layer, the exine, is made up of sporopollenin, one of the most resistant organic materials known; pollen grain exine has prominent apertures called germ pores where sporopollenin is absent. The inner wall, the intine, is a thin and continuous layer made up of cellulose and pectin. When the pollen grain is mature it contains two cells, the vegetative cell and the generative cell; the vegetative cell is bigger, has abundant food reserve and a large irregularly shaped nucleus, while the generative cell is small, floats in the cytoplasm of the vegetative cell, and is spindle shaped with dense cytoplasm and a nucleus. In over 60 per cent of angiosperms, pollen grains are shed at this 2-celled stage; in the remaining species, the generative cell divides mitotically to give rise to the two male gametes before pollen grains are shed (3-celled stage).
Step 1: Diploid MMC undergoes meiosis ⇒ four haploid microspores (tetrad).
Step 2: Microspores separate and develop walls ⇒ pollen grains.
Step 3: Pollen nucleus divides unequally ⇒ large vegetative cell + small generative cell; generative cell later forms two male gametes.
Why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number so that the male gametes are haploid; sporopollenin protects pollen, while germ pores allow the pollen tube to emerge.
Why not the others: (B) Tetrads arise by meiosis, so pollen is haploid. (C) Wall materials reversed. (D) Roles of the two cells reversed.
Key point: MMC (2n) → meiosis → microspores (n) → pollen with vegetative + generative cells; exine = sporopollenin.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting observations of the human ovary and oviduct in terms of oogenesis: meiotic arrest of the primary oocyte, ovulation of the secondary oocyte, and completion of meiosis II
questions.question: Microscope sections of a human ovary show many primary follicles with a large central cell arrested in prophase of meiosis I, and a mature Graafian follicle. A cell released at ovulation is examined later in the oviduct. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The cell released at ovulation is a mature ovum that has completed both meiotic divisions
B) New primary oocytes are formed throughout a woman's life by mitosis of oogonia

C) The primary oocytes were formed during fetal life and stay arrested in prophase I; in the Graafian follicle the primary oocyte completes meiosis I, forming a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body; the secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and completes meiosis II only after a sperm enters it, producing the ovum and a second polar body; so one primary oocyte yields only one ovum
D) Meiosis II is completed before ovulation, so the released cell has 46 chromosomes
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Primary oocytes arrested in prophase I since fetal life; secondary oocyte ovulated; meiosis II completed after sperm entry; one ovum per primary oocyte.
Concept: The process of formation of a mature female gamete is called oogenesis. Oogenesis is initiated during the embryonic development stage when a couple of million gamete mother cells (oogonia) are formed within each fetal ovary; no more oogonia are formed and added after birth. These cells start division and enter into prophase-I of the meiotic division and get temporarily arrested at that stage, called primary oocytes. Each primary oocyte then gets surrounded by a layer of granulosa cells and is called the primary follicle. A large number of these follicles degenerate during the phase from birth to puberty; therefore, at puberty only 60,000–80,000 primary follicles are left in each ovary. The primary oocyte within the tertiary follicle grows in size and completes its first meiotic division; it is an unequal division resulting in the formation of a large haploid secondary oocyte and a tiny first polar body. The tertiary follicle further changes into the mature follicle or Graafian follicle; the Graafian follicle now ruptures to release the secondary oocyte (ovum) from the ovary by the process called ovulation. The entry of sperm into the ovum induces the completion of the meiotic division of the secondary oocyte; the second meiotic division is also unequal and results in the formation of a second polar body and a haploid ovum (ootid).
Step 1: Arrest in prophase I seen in primary follicles ⇒ primary oocytes formed before birth.
Step 2: Meiosis I completed in the maturing follicle ⇒ secondary oocyte + first polar body.
Step 3: Meiosis II completed only on sperm entry ⇒ ovum + second polar body.
Why: Unequal divisions concentrate cytoplasm in one cell, so the single ovum has enough reserves for early development.
Why not the others: (A) The ovulated cell is a secondary oocyte arrested in meiosis II. (B) No new oogonia form after birth. (D) Meiosis II follows sperm entry, and the cell is haploid.
Key point: Primary oocyte (prophase I arrest, fetal) → secondary oocyte (ovulated) → ovum after sperm entry.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why polygenic traits show continuous variation, how the number of phenotypic classes depends on the number of genes, and the role of the environment
questions.question: Human skin colour and height vary continuously rather than falling into a few classes. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) Each such trait is controlled by a single gene with many alleles, each allele giving a separate class

B) Such polygenic traits are controlled by several genes whose alleles have additive effects, each dominant allele adding a small equal amount; with n genes, a cross between two individuals heterozygous for all of them gives 2n + 1 phenotypic classes and the two extreme classes each form (1/4)ⁿ of the progeny, so with many genes and environmental influence the classes merge into a continuous bell-shaped distribution
C) The traits show continuous variation because one allele is incompletely dominant over the other
D) Polygenic traits are not affected by the environment at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Several genes with additive effects; 2n + 1 classes; extremes (1/4)ⁿ each; environment blurs classes into a continuous curve.
Concept: Generally traits controlled by three or more genes are called polygenic traits; besides the involvement of multiple genes, polygenic inheritance also takes into account the influence of environment. Human skin colour is another classic example: assume that three genes A, B, C control skin colour in humans, with the dominant forms A, B and C responsible for dark skin colour and the recessive forms a, b and c for light skin colour; the genotype with all the dominant alleles (AABBCC) will have the darkest skin colour and that with all the recessive alleles (aabbcc) the lightest; a genotype with three dominant and three recessive alleles will have an intermediate skin colour. In this manner, the number of each type of allele in the genotype would determine the darkness or lightness of the skin of an individual. In polygenic inheritance the phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele, i.e. the effect of each allele is additive.
Formula/Principle: For n genes, the number of dominant alleles ranges from 0 to 2n ⇒ 2n + 1 classes; P(all recessive) = (1/4)ⁿ.
Step 1: One gene (Aa × Aa): 3 classes; extremes 1/4 each.
Step 2: Two genes: 5 classes (1 : 4 : 6 : 4 : 1); extremes 1/16 each.
Step 3: Three genes: 7 classes (1 : 6 : 15 : 20 : 15 : 6 : 1); extremes 1/64 each.
Why: Many small additive contributions, plus environmental effects such as nutrition and sunlight, produce a near-normal distribution in which neighbouring classes overlap.
Why not the others: (A) Multiple alleles of one gene give discrete classes, as in ABO groups. (C) Incomplete dominance at one locus gives only three classes. (D) Environment influences polygenic traits.
Key point: Polygenic traits: additive genes + environment ⇒ continuous variation; 2n + 1 classes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting Morgan's reciprocal crosses with the white-eye mutant of Drosophila as evidence that genes lie on chromosomes, and the parallel between Mendel's factors and chromosome behaviour
questions.question: In Drosophila, a red-eyed female crossed with a white-eyed male gives all red-eyed progeny, while the reciprocal cross, a white-eyed female with a red-eyed male, gives red-eyed females and white-eyed males. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The eye-colour gene lies on an autosome, so reciprocal crosses should differ

B) The eye-colour gene is carried on the X chromosome (males are XY and have only one copy), so in the second cross sons receive their only X, carrying the white allele, from the mother, while daughters also receive the father's X with the dominant red allele; such sex-linked results show that a gene follows a particular chromosome, supporting the chromosome theory of inheritance proposed by Sutton and Boveri, who noted that chromosomes, like Mendel's factors, occur in pairs, segregate at gamete formation and assort independently
C) The white allele is dominant in males and recessive in females
D) The results disprove Mendel's law of segregation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X-linked gene; sons get their X from the mother; supports the chromosome theory of Sutton and Boveri.
Concept: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behaviour of chromosomes was parallel to the behaviour of genes and used chromosome movement to explain Mendel's laws; they argued that the pairing and separation of a pair of chromosomes would lead to the segregation of a pair of factors they carried; Sutton united the knowledge of chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles and called it the chromosomal theory of inheritance. Experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance by Thomas Hunt Morgan and his colleagues led to discovering the basis for the variation that sexual reproduction produced; Morgan worked with the tiny fruit flies, Drosophila melanogaster, which were found very suitable for such studies because they could be grown on simple synthetic medium in the laboratory, they complete their life cycle in about two weeks, a single mating could produce a large number of progeny flies, there was a clear differentiation of the sexes, and they have many types of hereditary variations that can be seen with low power microscopes. In Drosophila the female is XX and the male XY; a gene on the X chromosome is present in two copies in females but only one copy in males.
Given: Cross 1: XᴿXᴿ × XʳY; Cross 2: XʳXʳ × XᴿY.
Step 1: Cross 1: daughters XᴿXʳ (red), sons XᴿY (red) ⇒ all red.
Step 2: Cross 2: daughters XᴿXʳ (red, X from father), sons XʳY (white, X from mother).
Step 3: Different outcomes of reciprocal crosses ⇒ gene tied to the X chromosome.
Why: A trait whose inheritance exactly follows the distribution of a visible chromosome is strong evidence that the gene is physically located on it.
Why not the others: (A) Autosomal genes give identical reciprocal crosses. (C) Dominance does not change with sex; males have only one allele. (D) Segregation is fully obeyed by the X-linked alleles.
Key point: Reciprocal crosses differ for X-linked genes ⇒ genes are on chromosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting an experiment in which mature mRNA is hybridised to its gene's DNA, together with the differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic transcription and processing
questions.question: A mature eukaryotic mRNA is allowed to pair with the single-stranded DNA of its own gene and viewed under the electron microscope; several loops of unpaired DNA appear. The same experiment with a bacterial gene shows no loops. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The loops are regions of DNA that code for the 5′ cap and poly(A) tail
B) Bacterial mRNA is processed more extensively than eukaryotic mRNA

C) The loops are introns: eukaryotic genes are split, and the primary transcript (hnRNA) has its introns removed by splicing, is capped with methyl guanosine triphosphate at the 5′ end and given a poly(A) tail at the 3′ end; in eukaryotes RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA precursors, polymerase I rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S) and polymerase III tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs; bacteria have one RNA polymerase (with σ for initiation and ρ for termination), their genes lack introns, and transcription and translation can be coupled in the cytoplasm
D) Eukaryotes have only one RNA polymerase, so their genes must contain loops
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Loops are introns removed by splicing; capping and tailing; three eukaryotic RNA polymerases; bacteria have one polymerase, no introns, coupled transcription–translation.
Concept: In bacteria there is a single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase that catalyses transcription of all types of RNA; RNA polymerase associates transiently with the initiation factor (σ) and termination factor (ρ) to initiate and terminate the transcription respectively. In bacteria, since the mRNA does not require any processing to become active, and since transcription and translation take place in the same compartment (there is no separation of cytosol and nucleus in bacteria), many times translation can begin much before the mRNA is fully transcribed. In eukaryotes there are at least three RNA polymerases in the nucleus (in addition to the RNA polymerase found in the organelles): RNA polymerase I transcribes rRNAs (28S, 18S and 5.8S), RNA polymerase III is responsible for transcription of tRNA, 5S rRNA and snRNAs (small nuclear RNAs), and RNA polymerase II transcribes the precursor of mRNA, the heterogeneous nuclear RNA (hnRNA). The primary transcripts contain both the exons and the introns and are non-functional; hence they are subjected to a process called splicing where the introns are removed and exons are joined in a defined order. hnRNA undergoes two additional processes called capping and tailing: in capping an unusual nucleotide (methyl guanosine triphosphate) is added to the 5′-end of hnRNA, and in tailing adenylate residues (200–300) are added at the 3′-end in a template-independent manner.
Step 1: Loops = DNA segments with no complementary sequence in mature mRNA.
Step 2: Such segments are introns, removed from the primary transcript by splicing.
Step 3: No loops for the bacterial gene ⇒ bacterial genes are not split.
Why: The hybridisation directly reveals which parts of the gene survive in the mature message, showing that eukaryotic genes are interrupted.
Why not the others: (A) The cap and tail are added without a DNA template. (B) Bacterial mRNA is not processed in this way. (D) Eukaryotes have three nuclear RNA polymerases.
Key point: Eukaryotic genes are split (exons + introns); hnRNA → splicing, capping, tailing → mRNA.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing homologous from analogous structures (divergent and convergent evolution), and the embryological and biochemical evidence for evolution
questions.question: Which explanation of evidences of evolution is correct?
options: A) Thorns of Bougainvillea and tendrils of Cucurbita are homologous, showing divergent evolution from a common ancestral structure; the eyes of the octopus and of mammals, and the flippers of penguins and dolphins, are analogous, performing similar functions but differing in anatomy because similar habitats selected similar adaptations (convergent evolution); sweet potato (root) and potato (stem) are likewise analogous; similarities in proteins and genes across organisms give biochemical evidence of common ancestry; Haeckel's proposal that embryos of higher animals pass through adult stages of other animals was disproved by Karl Ernst von Baer
B) The wings of a butterfly and of a bird are homologous, because both are used for flying
C) Analogous structures prove that the organisms share a recent common ancestor
D) The forelimbs of whales and bats are analogous, because they perform different functions
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Thorns/tendrils homologous (divergent); octopus/mammal eyes, penguin/dolphin flippers, sweet potato/potato analogous (convergent); biochemical similarities; Haeckel's idea disproved by von Baer.
Concept: Comparative anatomy and morphology shows similarities and differences among organisms of today and those that existed years ago. Whales, bats, cheetah and human share similarities in the pattern of bones of forelimbs; though these forelimbs perform different functions, they have similar anatomical structure — they are homologous organs, and homology indicates common ancestry; this is divergent evolution. In plants also, the thorns and tendrils of Bougainvillea and Cucurbita represent homology. Wings of butterfly and of birds look alike; they are not anatomically similar structures though they perform similar functions — analogous structures, the result of convergent evolution, different structures evolving for the same function and hence having similarity. Other examples of analogy are the eye of the octopus and of mammals, or the flippers of penguins and dolphins; sweet potato (root modification) and potato (stem modification) is another example. In the same line of argument, similarities in proteins and genes performing a given function among diverse organisms give clues to common ancestry; these biochemical similarities point to the same shared ancestry as structural similarities among diverse organisms. Embryological support for evolution was also proposed by Ernst Haeckel based upon the observation of certain features during the embryonic stage common to all vertebrates that are absent in adults; this proposal was disapproved on careful study performed by Karl Ernst von Baer, who noted that embryos never pass through the adult stages of other animals.
Why: Shared structure with different function reflects inheritance from a common ancestor; shared function with different structure reflects similar selection pressures on unrelated lineages.
Why not the others: (B) Butterfly and bird wings are analogous. (C) Analogy reflects convergence, not common ancestry. (D) Whale and bat forelimbs are homologous.
Key point: Homology → divergent evolution, common ancestry; analogy → convergent evolution.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Recognising stabilising, directional and disruptive selection from changes in the distribution of a trait, and interpreting the evolution of antibiotic and herbicide resistance
questions.question: Three populations are measured over many generations. In P the mean value of a trait stays the same while variation narrows; in Q the whole curve shifts towards larger values; in R individuals at both extremes increase while intermediates decline. Separately, bacteria exposed to an antibiotic become mostly resistant within a few years. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) P is directional, Q disruptive, R stabilising selection; resistance arose because the antibiotic induced mutations in every bacterium
B) All three are examples of genetic drift, since no environment change is mentioned
C) P is disruptive and R is stabilising; resistant bacteria arose only after exposure began

D) P shows stabilising selection (more individuals acquire the mean value), Q directional selection (individuals at one extreme are favoured, so the mean shifts) and R disruptive selection (both extremes favoured, possibly giving two peaks); antibiotic resistance evolved because resistant variants already present in the population survived and multiplied under the drug, an example of natural selection acting on pre-existing variation, as also seen with herbicide- and pesticide-resistant organisms
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) P stabilising, Q directional, R disruptive; resistance by selection of pre-existing variants.
Concept: Natural selection can lead to stabilisation (in which more individuals acquire the mean character value), directional change (more individuals acquire a value other than the mean character value) or disruption (more individuals acquire peripheral character values at both ends of the distribution curve). Excess use of herbicides, pesticides, etc. has only resulted in the selection of resistant varieties in a much lesser time scale; this is also true for microbes against which we employ antibiotics or drugs against eukaryotic organisms/cells — hence resistant organisms/cells are appearing in a time scale of months or years and not centuries; these are examples of evolution by anthropogenic action. Darwin's theory holds that variations which are heritable and which make resource utilisation better for a few will enable only those to reproduce and leave a greater number of progeny; the variants were already present, and the environment selects them.
Step 1: P: mean unchanged, spread reduced ⇒ intermediates favoured ⇒ stabilising.
Step 2: Q: mean shifts ⇒ one extreme favoured ⇒ directional.
Step 3: R: extremes increase ⇒ disruptive.
Why: Selection changes the frequency of existing heritable variants; the shape of the change reveals which phenotypes have higher fitness.
Why not the others: (A) Labels mismatched; antibiotics select, they do not create resistance in every cell. (B) Consistent, directional patterns indicate selection, not drift. (C) Labels swapped; resistant variants pre-exist.
Key point: Stabilising (mean favoured), directional (one extreme), disruptive (both extremes).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Linking the symptoms of three patients to the drug or habit involved — opioids, cocaine, tobacco smoking and chronic alcohol use — and their physiological effects
questions.question: Patient X has slowed body functions and constricted pupils after injecting a white crystalline powder obtained by acetylation of morphine. Patient Y feels euphoria and increased energy after snorting a drug from Erythroxylum coca. Patient Z, a heavy smoker, has raised blood pressure and reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) X used cannabinoids, Y used heroin, Z's problem is due to alcohol
B) X used cocaine, which is a depressant; Z's low oxygen capacity is due to nicotine binding to haemoglobin
C) Y used morphine, a stimulant that blocks dopamine transport

D) X used heroin (smack, diacetylmorphine), a depressant that binds opioid receptors in the CNS and gastrointestinal tract; Y used cocaine, which interferes with dopamine transport and stimulates the CNS, and excessive doses cause hallucinations; in Z, nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and noradrenaline, raising blood pressure and heart rate, while carbon monoxide in smoke binds haem and reduces oxygen-carrying capacity; chronic alcohol use, by contrast, damages the liver (cirrhosis) and the nervous system
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) X heroin (depressant, opioid receptors); Y cocaine (dopamine transport, stimulant); Z nicotine (adrenaline release) and CO (less O₂ carried).
Concept: Opioids are the drugs which bind to specific opioid receptors present in our central nervous system and gastrointestinal tract; heroin, commonly called smack, is chemically diacetylmorphine, a white, odourless, bitter crystalline compound obtained by acetylation of morphine, which is extracted from the latex of the poppy plant Papaver somniferum; generally taken by snorting and injection, heroin is a depressant and slows down body functions. Cocaine is obtained from the coca plant Erythroxylum coca, native to South America; it interferes with the transport of the neurotransmitter dopamine; cocaine, commonly called coke or crack, is usually snorted and has a potent stimulating action on the central nervous system, producing a sense of euphoria and increased energy; excessive dosage of cocaine causes hallucinations. Tobacco contains a large number of chemical substances including nicotine, an alkaloid; nicotine stimulates the adrenal gland to release adrenaline and nor-adrenaline into blood circulation, both of which raise blood pressure and increase heart rate; smoking increases carbon monoxide content in blood and reduces the concentration of haem-bound oxygen, causing oxygen deficiency in the body. The chronic use of drugs and alcohol damages the nervous system and the liver (cirrhosis).
Step 1: Acetylated morphine, depressant ⇒ heroin (X).
Step 2: Coca plant, euphoria, energy ⇒ cocaine (Y).
Step 3: Smoking: nicotine → adrenaline → high BP; CO → less haem-bound O₂ (Z).
Why: Each drug acts on a specific target — opioid receptors, dopamine transport or the adrenal medulla — which explains its pattern of symptoms.
Why not the others: (A) Drugs mismatched. (B) Cocaine is a stimulant, and CO, not nicotine, reduces oxygen carriage. (C) Morphine is a depressant opioid, not a stimulant from coca.
Key point: Heroin depresses (opioid receptors); cocaine stimulates (dopamine); smoking: nicotine ↑BP, CO ↓O₂.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing methods of introducing recombinant DNA into hosts — making bacteria competent with Ca²⁺ and heat shock, microinjection, biolistics and disarmed pathogen vectors
questions.question: Which comparison of methods for introducing recombinant DNA into host cells is correct?
options: A) Bacteria take up DNA freely through their hydrophobic membranes, so no treatment is needed
B) Microinjection is used mainly for bacteria, and heat shock mainly for plant cells

C) Because DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass through membranes, bacterial cells are made competent by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation such as calcium, then incubating with the DNA on ice, giving a brief heat shock at 42 °C and returning them to ice; in microinjection recombinant DNA is injected directly into the nucleus of an animal cell; in biolistics (gene gun) plant cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA; and disarmed pathogen vectors, such as Agrobacterium, deliver the recombinant DNA into the plant cells they infect
D) In biolistics, DNA is coated on calcium particles and injected into animal nuclei
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ca²⁺ + heat shock for bacteria; microinjection into animal nuclei; gene gun with gold or tungsten for plants; disarmed pathogen vectors.
Concept: Since DNA is a hydrophilic molecule, it cannot pass through cell membranes. In order to force bacteria to take up the plasmid, the bacterial cells must first be made 'competent' to take up DNA; this is done by treating them with a specific concentration of a divalent cation, such as calcium, which increases the efficiency with which DNA enters the bacterium through pores in its cell wall. Recombinant DNA can then be forced into such cells by incubating the cells with recombinant DNA on ice, followed by placing them briefly at 42 °C (heat shock), and then putting them back on ice; this enables the bacteria to take up the recombinant DNA. This is not the only way to introduce alien DNA into host cells. In a method known as micro-injection, recombinant DNA is directly injected into the nucleus of an animal cell. In another method, suitable for plants, cells are bombarded with high velocity micro-particles of gold or tungsten coated with DNA in a method known as biolistics or gene gun. And the last method uses 'disarmed pathogen' vectors, which when allowed to infect the cell, transfer the recombinant DNA into the host.
Why: Each method overcomes the membrane barrier in a way suited to the cell: chemical and thermal treatment for small bacteria, direct injection for large animal nuclei, and physical bombardment or natural infection for walled plant cells.
Why not the others: (A) DNA is hydrophilic and does not cross membranes freely. (B) Methods swapped. (D) Biolistics uses gold or tungsten and targets plant cells.
Key point: Competent bacteria (Ca²⁺ + heat shock); microinjection (animal cells); biolistics (plants); disarmed pathogens.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Reading a table comparing animal-derived insulin with genetically engineered human insulin, the structure of insulin and the processing of proinsulin
questions.question:
A table compares sources of insulin.

Property | Insulin from slaughtered pigs or cattle | Genetically engineered human insulin (Eli Lilly, 1983)
How chains are made | made in the animal pancreas | A and B chains made separately in E. coli from two DNA sequences inserted into plasmids
Effect on some patients | allergy or other reactions to the foreign protein | identical to human insulin
Supply | limited by animal availability | large-scale production possible

Which statement is correct?
options: A) Insulin has two short polypeptide chains, A and B, linked by disulphide bridges; in mammals it is synthesised as a prohormone, proinsulin, containing an extra C peptide that is removed during maturation; Eli Lilly made the A and B chains separately in E. coli, extracted them and combined them by creating disulphide bonds, avoiding the allergy problem of animal insulin
B) Insulin is a single polypeptide chain, so it can be expressed directly as one gene product
C) The C peptide is retained in mature insulin and is essential for its activity
D) Genetically engineered insulin is made by extracting insulin from human pancreas
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Two chains (A, B) linked by disulphide bridges; proinsulin with C peptide; chains made separately in E. coli and joined.
Concept: Management of adult-onset diabetes is possible by taking insulin at regular time intervals. Insulin used for diabetes was earlier extracted from the pancreas of slaughtered cattle and pigs; insulin from an animal source, though, caused some patients to develop allergy or other types of reactions to the foreign protein. Insulin consists of two short polypeptide chains, chain A and chain B, that are linked together by disulphide bridges. In mammals, including humans, insulin is synthesised as a pro-hormone (like a pro-enzyme, the pro-hormone also needs to be processed before it becomes a fully mature and functional hormone) which contains an extra stretch called the C peptide; this C peptide is not present in the mature insulin and is removed during maturation into insulin. The main challenge for production of insulin using rDNA techniques was getting insulin assembled into a mature form. In 1983, Eli Lilly, an American company, prepared two DNA sequences corresponding to A and B chains of human insulin and introduced them in plasmids of E. coli to produce insulin chains; chains A and B were produced separately, extracted and combined by creating disulphide bonds to form human insulin.
Given: Table of properties.
Step 1: Animal insulin is a foreign protein ⇒ allergic reactions in some patients.
Step 2: Mature insulin = A + B chains joined by S–S bonds; the C peptide is removed.
Step 3: Making A and B separately in E. coli and joining them gives functional human insulin without needing proinsulin processing.
Why: Bacteria cannot process proinsulin into insulin, so producing the two chains separately and joining them chemically bypassed this problem.
Why not the others: (B) Insulin has two chains. (C) The C peptide is absent from mature insulin. (D) The insulin is made by bacteria from introduced human DNA sequences.
Key point: Insulin = A + B chains (S–S); proinsulin has C peptide; Eli Lilly made A and B separately in E. coli.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Calculating growth under the exponential model from the intrinsic rate of increase, and the population size at which logistic growth is fastest
questions.question: A bacterial population with intrinsic rate of natural increase r = 0.693 h⁻¹ starts with 1000 cells and grows exponentially. In a second, resource-limited culture the population follows logistic growth with carrying capacity K = 8000 and the same r. Which statement is correct?
options: A) Exponential: 6000 cells after 6 h; logistic growth is fastest when N = K

B) Exponential: the population doubles every hour (ln 2/r = 1 h), so N = 1000 × 2⁶ = 64 000 after 6 h; logistic growth rate dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K) is greatest at N = K/2 = 4000, where it equals rK/4 ≈ 1386 cells h⁻¹, and it falls to zero as N approaches K
C) Exponential: 2000 cells after 6 h; the logistic curve is J-shaped
D) Exponential growth eventually levels off at K even when resources are unlimited
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 64 000 cells after 6 h; logistic growth fastest at N = K/2 = 4000, rate ≈ 1386 h⁻¹.
Concept: If in a habitat resources are unlimited, each species has the ability to realise fully its innate potential to grow in number; then the population grows in an exponential or geometric fashion: dN/dt = rN, whose integrated form is Nₜ = N₀e^(rt), where r is the intrinsic rate of natural increase; this gives a J-shaped curve. No population of any species in nature has at its disposal unlimited resources; a given habitat has enough resources to support a maximum possible number, beyond which no further growth is possible — the nature's carrying capacity (K). A population growing in a habitat with limited resources shows initially a lag phase, followed by phases of acceleration and deceleration and finally an asymptote, when the population density reaches the carrying capacity; a plot of N in relation to time t results in a sigmoid curve. This type of population growth is called Verhulst–Pearl logistic growth, described by dN/dt = rN((K − N)/K).
Given: r = 0.693 h⁻¹, N₀ = 1000, t = 6 h; K = 8000.
Formula/Principle: N = N₀e^(rt); doubling time = ln 2/r; logistic dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K).
Step 1: Doubling time = 0.693/0.693 = 1 h ⇒ 6 doublings in 6 h.
Step 2: N = 1000 × 2⁶ = 64 000.
Step 3: dN/dt is a downward parabola in N, maximum at N = K/2 = 4000: 0.693 × 4000 × 0.5 = 1386 h⁻¹.
Why: In the logistic model each added individual raises the number reproducing but reduces the resources left, so growth is fastest midway to K.
Why not the others: (A) Exponential growth multiplies, and logistic growth stops at K. (C) Wrong count, and the logistic curve is sigmoid. (D) Exponential growth has no ceiling.
Key point: Exponential N = N₀e^(rt) (J-shaped); logistic sigmoid, fastest at K/2.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: The order of the three steps of sexual reproduction in fungi and the dikaryotic phase, and the spores and examples of the major classes of fungi
questions.question: Which statement about the life cycles of fungi is correct?
options: A) In all fungi karyogamy occurs before plasmogamy, and meiosis follows immediately

B) Sexual reproduction involves three steps in order — plasmogamy (fusion of protoplasms of two motile or non-motile gametes), karyogamy (fusion of the two nuclei) and meiosis in the zygote to form haploid spores; in Ascomycetes and Basidiomycetes an intervening dikaryotic stage (n + n, two nuclei per cell) occurs before karyogamy; Phycomycetes (Mucor, Rhizopus, Albugo) form zygospores, Ascomycetes (Penicillium, Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora) form ascospores in asci and asexual conidia, Basidiomycetes (Agaricus, Ustilago, Puccinia) form basidiospores and have no sex organs, and Deuteromycetes are known only from asexual or vegetative phases
C) Basidiomycetes reproduce mainly by conidia and form ascospores
D) Deuteromycetes are named for their prominent sexual stage
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Plasmogamy → (dikaryon in asco- and basidiomycetes) → karyogamy → meiosis; spores and examples as listed.
Concept: Sexual reproduction in fungi is by oospores, ascospores and basidiospores; the various spores are produced in distinct structures called fruiting bodies. The sexual cycle involves the following three steps: (i) fusion of protoplasms between two motile or non-motile gametes, called plasmogamy; (ii) fusion of two nuclei, called karyogamy; (iii) meiosis in the zygote resulting in haploid spores. When a fungus reproduces sexually, two haploid hyphae of compatible mating types come together and fuse; in some fungi the fusion of two haploid cells immediately results in diploid cells (2n), whereas in other fungi (ascomycetes and basidiomycetes) an intervening dikaryotic stage (n + n, i.e. two nuclei per cell) occurs; such a condition is called a dikaryon and the phase is called the dikaryophase of the fungus; later, the parental nuclei fuse and the cells become diploid. Phycomycetes: asexual reproduction by zoospores (motile) or aplanospores (non-motile); zygospores formed by fusion of two gametes; e.g. Mucor, Rhizopus (bread mould) and Albugo (parasitic fungus on mustard). Ascomycetes (sac fungi): asexual spores are conidia produced exogenously on conidiophores; sexual spores are ascospores produced endogenously in sac-like asci; e.g. Aspergillus, Claviceps, Neurospora. Basidiomycetes: asexual spores are generally not found, but vegetative reproduction by fragmentation is common; sex organs are absent, but plasmogamy is brought about by fusion of two vegetative or somatic cells of different strains; basidiospores are produced exogenously on the basidium; e.g. Agaricus (mushroom), Ustilago (smut) and Puccinia (rust fungus). Deuteromycetes are commonly known as imperfect fungi because only the asexual or vegetative phases of these fungi are known.
Why: Plasmogamy and karyogamy can be separated in time, giving the dikaryotic phase characteristic of the higher fungi, before meiosis restores the haploid condition.
Why not the others: (A) Plasmogamy precedes karyogamy. (C) Basidiomycetes form basidiospores and generally lack asexual spores. (D) Deuteromycetes are imperfect fungi with no known sexual stage.
Key point: Plasmogamy → karyogamy → meiosis; dikaryon in Asco- and Basidiomycetes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the members of the endomembrane system — rough and smooth ER, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes and vacuoles — and why mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are excluded
questions.question: Which comparison of cell organelles is correct?
options: A) Mitochondria and chloroplasts belong to the endomembrane system because they have membranes
B) The smooth ER is the main site of protein synthesis, and the rough ER of lipid synthesis
C) Lysosomal enzymes work best at alkaline pH, and the vacuole occupies about 10 per cent of a plant cell

D) The ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles form the endomembrane system because their functions are coordinated, whereas mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included; ribosome-bearing rough ER makes and secretes proteins, while smooth ER synthesises lipids and, in animal cells, steroidal hormones; the Golgi apparatus receives materials at its cis (forming) face and releases them from the trans (maturing) face, and is the site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids; lysosomes, formed from the Golgi, contain hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH; and the plant vacuole, bounded by the tonoplast, may occupy up to 90 per cent of the cell volume
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vacuoles form the endomembrane system; RER proteins, SER lipids; cis and trans faces; acidic lysosomal enzymes; vacuole up to 90 %.
Concept: While each of the membranous organelles is distinct in terms of its structure and function, many of these are considered together as an endomembrane system because their functions are coordinated; the endomembrane system includes the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Since the functions of the mitochondria, chloroplast and peroxisomes are not coordinated with the above components, these are not considered as part of the endomembrane system. ER bearing ribosomes on its surface is called rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER), frequently observed in cells actively involved in protein synthesis and secretion; ER that does not bear ribosomes appears smooth (SER) and is the major site for synthesis of lipids; in animal cells lipid-like steroidal hormones are synthesised in SER. The Golgi cisternae are concentrically arranged near the nucleus with distinct convex cis or forming face and concave trans or maturing face; materials to be packaged in the form of vesicles from the ER fuse with the cis face of the Golgi apparatus and move towards the maturing face; the Golgi apparatus is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids. Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicular structures formed by the process of packaging in the Golgi apparatus; they are very rich in almost all types of hydrolytic enzymes (hydrolases — lipases, proteases, carbohydrases) optimally active at the acidic pH. The vacuole is bound by a single membrane called the tonoplast; in plant cells the vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of the cell.
Why: The endomembrane organelles exchange membrane and contents by vesicle traffic, forming one functional pathway from synthesis to processing to delivery.
Why not the others: (A) Mitochondria and chloroplasts function independently of this system. (B) Roles of RER and SER reversed. (C) Lysosomal enzymes need acidic pH; vacuoles can fill up to 90 % of the cell.
Key point: Endomembrane system = ER + Golgi + lysosomes + vacuoles (coordinated functions).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting water molecules released in forming a triglyceride and a polysaccharide, carbons in common fatty acids, and the nature of glycosidic and ester bonds
questions.question: Which set of counts and statements about lipids and carbohydrates is correct?
options: A) Forming one triglyceride from glycerol and three fatty acids releases 3 molecules of water (three ester bonds); joining 100 glucose units into an unbranched chain releases 99 molecules of water (99 glycosidic bonds); palmitic acid has 16 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon and arachidonic acid 20; lecithin is a phospholipid containing phosphorus and a phosphorylated organic compound; starch forms helical secondary structures that hold iodine, giving a blue colour, whereas cellulose does not
B) A triglyceride releases 1 water molecule; 100 glucose units release 100
C) Palmitic acid has 20 carbons and arachidonic acid 16; lecithin contains no phosphorus
D) Cellulose gives a blue colour with iodine because of its helices
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3 water molecules per triglyceride; 99 for a 100-glucose chain; palmitic C₁₆, arachidonic C₂₀; lecithin a phospholipid; starch–iodine blue.
Concept: Lipids are generally water insoluble; they could be simple fatty acids, which have a carboxyl group attached to an R group; the R group could be a methyl, ethyl or a higher number of –CH₂ groups (1 carbon to 19 carbons); for example, palmitic acid has 16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon, and arachidonic acid has 20 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon. Many lipids have both glycerol and fatty acids; here the fatty acids are found esterified with glycerol and can then be monoglycerides, diglycerides and triglycerides. Some lipids have phosphorous and a phosphorylated organic compound in them — these are phospholipids, found in cell membranes; lecithin is one example. A polysaccharide is a long chain of sugars; in a polysaccharide the individual monosaccharides are linked by a glycosidic bond, formed by dehydration. Starch forms helical secondary structures; in fact, starch can hold I₂ molecules in the helical portion, and the starch–I₂ is blue in colour; cellulose does not contain complex helices and hence cannot hold I₂.
Given: Glycerol + 3 fatty acids; 100 glucose units in a linear chain.
Formula/Principle: Each ester or glycosidic bond formed by condensation releases one H₂O; n units in a chain are joined by n − 1 bonds.
Step 1: Triglyceride: 3 ester bonds ⇒ 3 H₂O.
Step 2: Linear chain of 100 glucose units: 99 glycosidic bonds ⇒ 99 H₂O.
Step 3: Carbon counts: palmitic 16, arachidonic 20 (including the carboxyl carbon).
Why: Condensation reactions build biological polymers and esters by removing water at each new linkage; hydrolysis reverses this.
Why not the others: (B) Miscounts the bonds. (C) Carbon numbers swapped; lecithin contains phosphorus. (D) Cellulose lacks helices and does not hold iodine.
Key point: Each condensation link releases one H₂O; n units → n − 1 bonds; starch + I₂ = blue.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting ¹⁴CO₂ labelling and growth observations to distinguish C₃ and C₄ plants, Kranz anatomy, and why C₄ plants show no photorespiration
questions.question: Leaves of wheat and of maize are exposed to ¹⁴CO₂ for a few seconds. In wheat the label appears first in 3-phosphoglycerate (PGA); in maize it appears first in oxaloacetate (OAA). At high light and high temperature, maize also shows higher productivity. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) Maize is a C₃ plant whose RuBisCO fixes CO₂ directly into OAA
B) Wheat fixes CO₂ first into a four-carbon acid, and maize into a three-carbon acid

C) Maize is a C₄ plant: in its mesophyll cells PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into the 4-carbon OAA, which is converted to other 4-carbon acids (malic or aspartic) and moved to the bundle sheath cells (Kranz anatomy), where CO₂ is released and fixed by RuBisCO in the Calvin cycle; the high CO₂ concentration around RuBisCO prevents its oxygenase activity, so C₄ plants show no photorespiration and tolerate higher temperatures and light; wheat is a C₃ plant in which RuBisCO fixes CO₂ into PGA
D) The difference shows that maize does not use the Calvin cycle at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Maize is C₄ (PEP carboxylase → OAA in mesophyll; Calvin cycle in bundle sheath; no photorespiration); wheat is C₃ (RuBisCO → PGA).
Concept: Plants adapted to dry tropical regions have the C₄ pathway; though these plants have the C₄ oxaloacetic acid as the first CO₂ fixation product, they use the C₃ pathway or the Calvin cycle as the main biosynthetic pathway. C₄ plants are special: they have a special type of leaf anatomy, they tolerate higher temperatures, they show a response to high light intensities, they lack a process called photorespiration and have greater productivity of biomass. The particularly large cells around the vascular bundles of the C₄ pathway plants are called bundle sheath cells, and leaves which have such anatomy are said to have 'Kranz' anatomy. The primary CO₂ acceptor is a 3-carbon molecule phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP) present in the mesophyll cells, and the enzyme responsible for this fixation is PEP carboxylase or PEPcase; the mesophyll cells lack RuBisCO enzyme. The C₄ acid OAA is formed in the mesophyll cells; it then forms other 4-carbon compounds like malic acid or aspartic acid, which are transported to the bundle sheath cells, where they are broken down to release CO₂ and a 3-carbon molecule. The CO₂ released in the bundle sheath cells enters the C₃ or Calvin pathway, common to all plants; the bundle sheath cells are rich in RuBisCO but lack PEPcase. In C₄ plants photorespiration does not occur because they have a mechanism that increases the concentration of CO₂ at the enzyme site; this takes place when the C₄ acid from the mesophyll is broken down in the bundle sheath cells to release CO₂, which increases the intracellular concentration of CO₂, ensuring that RuBisCO functions as a carboxylase, minimising the oxygenase activity.
Step 1: First labelled product PGA (3C) ⇒ RuBisCO fixation ⇒ C₃ (wheat).
Step 2: First labelled product OAA (4C) ⇒ PEPcase fixation ⇒ C₄ (maize).
Step 3: CO₂ concentrated around RuBisCO in bundle sheath ⇒ no photorespiration ⇒ higher productivity in hot, bright conditions.
Why: The identity of the earliest labelled compound reveals the first carboxylating enzyme; spatial separation of the two carboxylations is what lets C₄ plants avoid photorespiration.
Why not the others: (A) RuBisCO gives PGA, and maize uses PEPcase first. (B) Reversed. (D) C₄ plants use the Calvin cycle in the bundle sheath.
Key point: C₃: first product PGA; C₄: first product OAA, Kranz anatomy, no photorespiration.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Explaining agricultural and horticultural uses of auxins, gibberellins and cytokinins from their physiological effects
questions.question: Which set of applications is correctly explained?
options: A) Spraying gibberellins on sugarcane reduces stem length, so it is used to dwarf the crop
B) 2,4-D kills monocot weeds selectively while sparing dicot crops

C) Auxins induce parthenocarpy (e.g. in tomatoes) and prevent premature fruit and leaf drop; 2,4-D, a synthetic auxin, kills dicot weeds and is used to weed-free lawns; gibberellins elongate the stem, so spraying sugarcane increases yield by about 20 tonnes per acre, and they hasten malting in brewing and cause bolting in rosette plants such as beet and cabbage; cytokinins promote cell division, help overcome apical dominance, promote nutrient mobilisation and so delay leaf senescence
D) Cytokinins hasten leaf senescence and strengthen apical dominance
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Auxin: parthenocarpy, prevents drop, 2,4-D kills dicots; gibberellin: sugarcane yield, malting, bolting; cytokinin: cell division, overcomes apical dominance, delays senescence.
Concept: Auxins help to initiate rooting in stem cuttings; they promote flowering, e.g. in pineapples; they help to prevent fruit and leaf drop at early stages but promote the abscission of older mature leaves and fruits. In most higher plants, the growing apical bud inhibits the growth of the lateral (axillary) buds, a phenomenon called apical dominance. Auxins also induce parthenocarpy, e.g. in tomatoes; they are widely used as herbicides — 2,4-D, widely used to kill dicotyledonous weeds, does not affect mature monocotyledonous plants and is used to prepare weed-free lawns by gardeners. Gibberellins cause an increase in length of axis and are thus used to increase the length of grape stalks; since sugarcane stores carbohydrate as sugar in its stems, spraying a sugarcane crop with gibberellins increases the length of the stem, thus increasing the yield by as much as 20 tonnes per acre. Gibberellins are also used to speed up the malting process in the brewing industry, and they promote bolting (internode elongation just prior to flowering) in beet, cabbages and many plants with rosette habit. Cytokinins have specific effects on cytokinesis; they help to produce new leaves, chloroplasts in leaves, lateral shoot growth and adventitious shoot formation; cytokinins help overcome the apical dominance; they promote nutrient mobilisation, which helps in the delay of leaf senescence.
Why: Each application uses a known effect — auxin on fruit set and selective toxicity, gibberellin on internode elongation and enzyme induction in seeds, cytokinin on cell division and nutrient sinks.
Why not the others: (A) Gibberellins lengthen stems. (B) 2,4-D kills dicots, sparing monocots. (D) Cytokinins delay senescence and counter apical dominance.
Key point: Auxin (parthenocarpy, 2,4-D); gibberellin (stem elongation, malting, bolting); cytokinin (delays senescence).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting shifts of the oxygen dissociation curve with pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature, and the forms in which carbon dioxide is transported in blood
questions.question: Blood samples are equilibrated at the same pO₂ (40 mm Hg) under two conditions: sample 1 at low pCO₂, normal pH and 37 °C; sample 2 at high pCO₂, lower pH and higher temperature. Sample 2 shows lower percentage saturation of haemoglobin. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) High pCO₂ increases the binding of oxygen to haemoglobin, so sample 2 should be more saturated
B) The difference shows that CO₂ is mostly transported dissolved in plasma
C) Oxygen binding depends only on pO₂, so the result must be an experimental error

D) The oxygen dissociation curve is sigmoid and shifts to the right when pCO₂, H⁺ concentration and temperature rise, as in the tissues, so haemoglobin releases more oxygen there; in the alveoli, high pO₂, low pCO₂, lower H⁺ and lower temperature favour oxyhaemoglobin formation; about 20–25 per cent of CO₂ is carried as carbamino-haemoglobin, about 70 per cent as bicarbonate (formed with the help of carbonic anhydrase in RBCs) and about 7 per cent dissolved in plasma
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Right shift with high pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature favours O₂ release in tissues; CO₂ carried 20–25 % carbamino, ~70 % bicarbonate, ~7 % dissolved.
Concept: Haemoglobin is a red coloured iron-containing pigment present in the RBCs; O₂ can bind with haemoglobin in a reversible manner to form oxyhaemoglobin, and each haemoglobin molecule can carry a maximum of four molecules of O₂. Binding of oxygen with haemoglobin is primarily related to the partial pressure of O₂; partial pressure of CO₂, hydrogen ion concentration and temperature are the other factors which can interfere with this binding. A sigmoid curve is obtained when percentage saturation of haemoglobin with O₂ is plotted against pO₂; this curve is called the oxygen dissociation curve and is highly useful in studying the effect of factors like pCO₂, H⁺ concentration, etc. on the binding of O₂ with haemoglobin. In the alveoli, where there is high pO₂, low pCO₂, lesser H⁺ concentration and lower temperature, the factors are all favourable for the formation of oxyhaemoglobin, whereas in the tissues, where low pO₂, high pCO₂, high H⁺ concentration and higher temperature exist, the conditions are favourable for dissociation of oxygen from the oxyhaemoglobin. CO₂ is carried by haemoglobin as carbamino-haemoglobin (about 20–25 per cent); RBCs contain a very high concentration of the enzyme carbonic anhydrase, and minute quantities of this enzyme are present in the plasma too, facilitating CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ HCO₃⁻ + H⁺; nearly 20–25 per cent of CO₂ is transported by RBCs whereas 70 per cent of it is carried as bicarbonate, and about 7 per cent of CO₂ is carried in a dissolved state through plasma.
Step 1: Same pO₂, lower saturation in sample 2 ⇒ curve shifted right.
Step 2: Conditions of sample 2 resemble active tissues ⇒ oxygen unloading favoured.
Step 3: Sample 1 resembles alveolar conditions ⇒ loading favoured.
Why: These conditions reduce haemoglobin's affinity for O₂ exactly where O₂ is needed, improving delivery to metabolically active tissues.
Why not the others: (A) High pCO₂ lowers O₂ affinity. (B) Only about 7 % of CO₂ travels dissolved. (C) pCO₂, H⁺ and temperature also affect binding.
Key point: Tissue conditions (↑pCO₂, ↑H⁺, ↑T) shift the curve right ⇒ O₂ unloading.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Tracing the path of blood through the chambers and valves of the human heart in double circulation, and the effect of a hole in the interatrial septum
questions.question: A dye is injected into the superior vena cava of a healthy person and its route through the heart is followed by imaging. In a second person with a hole in the interatrial septum, some dye appears in the left atrium within the first beat. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) In the healthy heart the dye passes right atrium → (tricuspid valve) right ventricle → (semilunar valve) pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → (bicuspid/mitral valve) left ventricle → (semilunar valve) aorta, so it passes through the heart twice in one complete circuit (double circulation); in the second person the hole lets deoxygenated blood from the right atrium mix with oxygenated blood in the left atrium, so the separation of the two circulations is lost
B) The dye passes first into the left atrium in all people, because the vena cava opens there
C) The tricuspid valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle
D) A hole in the interatrial septum improves oxygen delivery by allowing blood to bypass the lungs
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) RA → RV → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary veins → LA → LV → aorta (double circulation); a septal hole mixes deoxygenated and oxygenated blood.
Concept: The heart has four chambers, two relatively small upper chambers called atria and two larger lower chambers called ventricles. A thin, muscular wall called the inter-atrial septum separates the right and the left atria, whereas a thick-walled inter-ventricular septum separates the left and the right ventricles. The atrium and the ventricle of the same side are also separated by a thick fibrous tissue called the atrio-ventricular septum; each of these septa is provided with an opening through which the two chambers of the same side are connected. The opening between the right atrium and the right ventricle is guarded by a valve formed of three muscular flaps or cusps, the tricuspid valve, whereas a bicuspid or mitral valve guards the opening between the left atrium and the left ventricle. The openings of the right and the left ventricles into the pulmonary artery and the aorta respectively are provided with the semilunar valves; the valves in the heart allow the flow of blood only in one direction. The deoxygenated blood pumped into the pulmonary artery is passed on to the lungs, from where the oxygenated blood is carried by the pulmonary veins into the left atrium; this pathway constitutes the pulmonary circulation. The oxygenated blood entering the aorta is carried by a network of arteries, arterioles and capillaries to the tissues, from where the deoxygenated blood is collected by a system of venules, veins and vena cava and emptied into the right atrium; this is the systemic circulation. In humans, two separate circulatory pathways are found — this is called double circulation.
Step 1: Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs.
Step 2: Lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.
Step 3: A septal hole short-circuits the right atrium to the left atrium ⇒ mixing.
Why: Complete separation of the right and left hearts keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood apart, maximising oxygen delivery.
Why not the others: (B) Venae cavae open into the right atrium. (C) The tricuspid valve is on the right side. (D) Bypassing the lungs lowers the oxygen content of systemic blood.
Key point: Double circulation: pulmonary (RV → lungs → LA) and systemic (LV → body → RA).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing cortical and juxtamedullary nephrons and the functions of the proximal convoluted tubule, Henle's loop, distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct
questions.question: Which comparison of nephrons and their parts is correct?
options: A) Cortical nephrons have very long loops of Henle that run deep into the medulla, while juxtamedullary nephrons have short loops

B) In the majority (cortical) nephrons the loop of Henle is short and extends only slightly into the medulla, while juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops running deep into the medulla; the PCT reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients and 70–80 per cent of electrolytes and water; the descending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, the ascending limb impermeable to water but permitting transport of electrolytes; the DCT conditionally reabsorbs Na⁺ and water and secretes H⁺, K⁺ and NH₃; and the collecting duct reabsorbs large amounts of water to concentrate the urine
C) The ascending limb of Henle's loop is permeable to water and impermeable to electrolytes
D) Glucose is reabsorbed mainly in the collecting duct
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cortical nephrons short loops, juxtamedullary long loops; PCT 70–80 % reabsorption; limbs with opposite permeabilities; DCT conditional reabsorption; collecting duct concentrates urine.
Concept: In the majority of nephrons, the loop of Henle is too short and extends only very little into the medulla; such nephrons are called cortical nephrons. In some of the nephrons, the loop of Henle is very long and runs deep into the medulla; these nephrons are called juxta medullary nephrons. Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) is lined by simple cuboidal brush border epithelium which increases the surface area for reabsorption; nearly all of the essential nutrients, and 70–80 per cent of electrolytes and water, are reabsorbed by this segment; PCT also helps to maintain the pH and ionic balance of the body fluids by selective secretion of hydrogen ions, ammonia and potassium ions into the filtrate and by absorption of HCO₃⁻ from it. Henle's loop: reabsorption in this segment is minimum; the descending limb of the loop of Henle is permeable to water but almost impermeable to electrolytes, which concentrates the filtrate as it moves down; the ascending limb is impermeable to water but allows transport of electrolytes actively or passively, so the filtrate gets diluted as it moves up. Distal convoluted tubule (DCT): conditional reabsorption of Na⁺ and water takes place in this segment; DCT is also capable of reabsorption of HCO₃⁻ and selective secretion of hydrogen and potassium ions and NH₃ to maintain the pH and sodium–potassium balance in blood. Collecting duct: this long duct extends from the cortex of the kidney to the inner parts of the medulla; large amounts of water could be reabsorbed from this region to produce a concentrated urine.
Why: Long loops of juxtamedullary nephrons build the medullary osmotic gradient used by the collecting duct to concentrate urine; segment-specific permeabilities divide the work of reabsorption.
Why not the others: (A) Loop lengths reversed. (C) Permeabilities of the ascending limb reversed. (D) Glucose is reabsorbed in the PCT.
Key point: Cortical (short loops) vs juxtamedullary (long loops); PCT reabsorbs most; collecting duct concentrates urine.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the products of heating ethanol with concentrated sulphuric acid at two temperatures, the three-step dehydration mechanism, and the order of ease of dehydration of alcohols
questions.question: Ethanol heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ gives mainly diethyl ether at 413 K but mainly ethene at 443 K. Tertiary butyl alcohol dehydrates readily at about 358 K with 20 % H₃PO₄. Which interpretation of these observations is correct?
options: A) Dehydration begins with loss of OH⁻ from the neutral alcohol, so primary alcohols react fastest

B) Dehydration of alcohols is acid catalysed: (i) the alcohol is protonated to form an oxonium ion, (ii) water leaves in the slow, rate-determining step to give a carbocation, (iii) a proton is lost to form the alkene; at the lower temperature a second alcohol molecule attacks the protonated alcohol (nucleophilic substitution) to give ether, while higher temperature favours elimination; since 3° carbocations are most stable, the ease of dehydration is 3° > 2° > 1°
C) Ether forms at higher temperature and ethene at lower temperature
D) Tertiary alcohols dehydrate with most difficulty because their carbocations are least stable
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Protonation → slow loss of water (carbocation) → deprotonation; ether at 413 K by substitution, alkene at 443 K by elimination; 3° > 2° > 1°.
Concept: Alcohols undergo dehydration (removal of a molecule of water) to form alkenes on treating with a protic acid, e.g. concentrated H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄, or catalysts such as anhydrous zinc chloride or alumina. Ethanol undergoes dehydration by heating it with concentrated H₂SO₄ at 443 K; secondary and tertiary alcohols are dehydrated under milder conditions, and the relative ease of dehydration of alcohols follows the order tertiary > secondary > primary. The mechanism of dehydration of ethanol involves the following steps: Step 1 — formation of protonated alcohol; Step 2 — formation of carbocation, the slowest step and hence the rate determining step; Step 3 — formation of ethene by elimination of a proton. Alcohols undergo dehydration in the presence of protic acids to give alkenes or ethers depending on the reaction conditions: ethanol at 413 K gives ethoxyethane, the formation of ether being a nucleophilic bimolecular reaction involving the attack of an alcohol molecule on a protonated alcohol.
Step 1: CH₃CH₂OH + H⁺ ⇌ CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ (fast).
Step 2: At 413 K: CH₃CH₂OH attacks CH₃CH₂OH₂⁺ ⇒ C₂H₅OC₂H₅ + H₂O + H⁺ (substitution).
Step 3: At 443 K: loss of water and a proton ⇒ CH₂=CH₂ (elimination favoured by higher temperature).
Why: Converting –OH into –OH₂⁺ creates a good leaving group (water); the stability of the carbocation intermediate governs how easily each alcohol dehydrates.
Why not the others: (A) OH⁻ is a poor leaving group; protonation is needed, and 1° alcohols react slowest. (C) Temperatures reversed. (D) 3° carbocations are most stable, so 3° alcohols dehydrate most easily.
Key point: Acid dehydration: protonation, slow carbocation, deprotonation; 3° > 2° > 1°.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking carbonyl compounds by reactivity towards nucleophilic addition using steric and electronic effects, and the addition of HCN and sodium hydrogensulphite
questions.question: Which ranking of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition, with its explanation, is correct?
options: A) CH₃COCH₃ > CH₃CHO > HCHO, because alkyl groups increase the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
B) Benzaldehyde is more reactive than propanal because the benzene ring withdraws electrons by resonance

C) HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃, and propanal > benzaldehyde: alkyl groups hinder the approach of the nucleophile sterically and reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon by electron donation, while in benzaldehyde resonance with the ring makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic; nucleophilic addition, e.g. of HCN (catalysed by base, giving cyanohydrins) or of NaHSO₃ (giving crystalline bisulphite addition products used to purify aldehydes), proceeds through attack of the nucleophile to form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate
D) Ketones are more reactive than aldehydes because they have two electron-donating groups
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃; propanal > benzaldehyde; steric and electronic reasons; cyanohydrins and bisulphite adducts.
Concept: Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition reactions due to steric and electronic reasons. Sterically, the presence of two relatively large substituents in ketones hinders the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon more than in aldehydes having only one such substituent. Electronically, aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because two alkyl groups reduce the electrophilicity of the carbonyl carbon more effectively than one. Aromatic aldehydes are less reactive than aliphatic aldehydes: the polarity of the carbonyl group is reduced in benzaldehyde due to resonance, and hence it is less reactive than propanal. In nucleophilic addition, a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon atom of the polar carbonyl group from a direction approximately perpendicular to the plane of sp² hybridised orbitals; hybridisation of carbon changes from sp² to sp³ in this process and a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate is produced, which captures a proton. Aldehydes and ketones react with HCN to yield cyanohydrins; this reaction occurs very slowly with pure HCN and is catalysed by a base, which generates the stronger nucleophile CN⁻. Sodium hydrogensulphite adds to aldehydes and ketones to form the addition products; the hydrogensulphite addition compound is water soluble and can be converted back to the original carbonyl compound by treating it with dilute mineral acid or alkali, so these are useful for separation and purification of aldehydes.
Step 1: HCHO: no alkyl groups ⇒ least hindered, most electrophilic.
Step 2: CH₃CHO: one methyl; CH₃COCH₃: two methyls ⇒ order HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃.
Step 3: Benzaldehyde: resonance donation from the ring lowers the carbonyl δ⁺ ⇒ less reactive than propanal.
Why: A more positive and less crowded carbonyl carbon is attacked more easily by the nucleophile.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed; alkyl groups donate electrons. (B) Resonance reduces reactivity of benzaldehyde. (D) Ketones are less reactive.
Key point: Nucleophilic addition: HCHO > RCHO > RCOR; aliphatic > aromatic aldehydes.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Counting exchange pairs in half-filled and partly filled subshells, and using exchange energy to explain anomalies in ionisation enthalpy of N/O and P/S
questions.question: The first ionisation enthalpy of nitrogen (1402 kJ mol⁻¹) is higher than that of oxygen (1314 kJ mol⁻¹), and that of phosphorus is higher than that of sulphur. Counting the possible exchanges of parallel-spin electrons, how many exchange pairs does a d⁵ configuration have compared with d⁴, and what explains the ionisation enthalpy anomaly?
options: A) d⁵ has 10 exchange pairs and d⁴ has 6; half-filled subshells are extra stable because of the larger exchange energy and symmetrical distribution; N (2p³) and P (3p³) have half-filled p subshells, while in O (2p⁴) and S (3p⁴) the fourth p electron is paired in an already occupied orbital, so electron–electron repulsion makes it easier to remove; hence IE₁ of N > O and P > S
B) d⁵ has 5 pairs and d⁴ has 4; the anomaly arises because oxygen is larger than nitrogen
C) d⁵ has 10 pairs and d⁴ has 10; the anomaly is due to higher nuclear charge of oxygen
D) d⁵ has 20 pairs and d⁴ has 12; half-filled subshells are less stable
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 10 and 6 exchange pairs; half-filled stability and pairing repulsion explain IE₁ N > O and P > S.
Concept: The completely filled and completely half-filled subshells are stable due to the following reasons: (i) symmetrical distribution of electrons — the completely filled or half-filled subshells have a symmetrical distribution of electrons and are therefore more stable; electrons in the same subshell have equal energy but different spatial distribution, so their shielding of one another is relatively small and the electrons are more strongly attracted by the nucleus; (ii) exchange energy — the stabilising effect arises whenever two or more electrons with the same spin are present in the degenerate orbitals of a subshell; these electrons tend to exchange their positions and the energy released due to this exchange is called exchange energy. The number of exchanges that can take place is maximum when the subshell is either half-filled or completely filled; as a result the exchange energy is maximum and so is the stability. Nitrogen has a higher first ionisation enthalpy than oxygen although oxygen has a larger nuclear charge: in nitrogen the three 2p electrons reside in different atomic orbitals (Hund's rule), whereas in oxygen two of the four 2p electrons must occupy the same 2p orbital, resulting in increased electron–electron repulsion; consequently it is easier to remove the fourth 2p electron from oxygen than one of the three 2p electrons from nitrogen.
Given: d⁵ and d⁴ high-spin configurations, all spins parallel.
Formula/Principle: Number of exchange pairs among n parallel electrons = nC₂ = n(n − 1)/2.
Step 1: d⁵: 5C₂ = 10.
Step 2: d⁴: 4C₂ = 6.
Step 3: The gain of 4 exchanges from d⁴ to d⁵ is the source of the extra stability of half-filled sets, as in N (2p³) and P (3p³).
Why: Removing an electron from a half-filled set destroys exchange stabilisation, while removing the paired fourth electron of O or S relieves repulsion, so less energy is needed.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) Wrong counts; O is smaller than N. (C) Wrong d⁴ count; higher nuclear charge would raise, not lower, IE of O.
Key point: Exchange pairs = nC₂ (d⁵ = 10, d⁴ = 6); half-filled p³ ⇒ IE₁ N > O, P > S.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Moseley's relation between X-ray frequency and atomic number, the IUPAC provisional names of elements with Z > 100, and locating an element from its atomic number
questions.question: Moseley plotted the square root of the frequency of characteristic X-rays of elements against atomic number. Which conclusion and naming statement is correct?
options: A) The plot of √ν against atomic mass was a straight line, so atomic mass is the fundamental property
B) Element 104 has the IUPAC provisional name unnilennium and symbol Une
C) Element 114 lies in period 6 and group 16

D) The plot of √ν against atomic number Z is a straight line, but not against atomic mass, so Z is the more fundamental property, giving the modern periodic law; under the IUPAC provisional naming scheme digits are named nil (0), un (1), bi (2), tri (3), quad (4), pent (5), hex (6), sept (7), oct (8), enn (9) and the suffix -ium is added, so element 104 is unnilquadium (Unq) and 110 ununnilium (Uun); element 114, with configuration ending 7s² 7p², lies in period 7 and group 14
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) √ν vs Z is linear (modern periodic law); 104 = Unq, 110 = Uun; element 114 in period 7, group 14.
Concept: In 1913, the English physicist Henry Moseley observed regularities in the characteristic X-ray spectra of the elements; a plot of √ν (where ν is the frequency of X-rays emitted) against atomic number (Z) gave a straight line and not the plot of √ν vs atomic mass. He thereby showed that the atomic number is a more fundamental property of an element than its atomic mass; Mendeleev's periodic law was therefore accordingly modified, and this is known as the modern periodic law: the physical and chemical properties of the elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers. The IUPAC nomenclature for elements with Z > 100 uses roots for the digits: 0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn; the roots are put together in order of digits which make up the atomic number, and 'ium' is added at the end; the symbol is formed from the first letters of the roots. Thus 101 is unnilunium (Unu), 104 unnilquadium (Unq) and 110 ununnilium (Uun). The period of an element corresponds to the principal quantum number of its valence shell, and for p-block elements the group number is 10 + the number of valence electrons.
Step 1: 104 → un-nil-quad-ium ⇒ Unq; 110 → un-un-nil-ium ⇒ Uun.
Step 2: Z = 114: after Rn (86), 7s² 5f¹⁴ 6d¹⁰ 7p² ⇒ n = 7 ⇒ period 7.
Step 3: Valence electrons in s and p = 4 ⇒ group 10 + 4 = 14.
Why: X-ray frequency depends on nuclear charge, so a straight-line relation with Z shows that nuclear charge, not mass, orders the elements.
Why not the others: (A) The straight line is with Z. (B) Une would be 109. (C) Element 114 is in period 7, group 14.
Key point: √ν ∝ Z (Moseley); IUPAC roots nil-un-bi-tri-quad…; Z = 114 → period 7, group 14.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting experimental bond lengths in ozone and the carbonate ion through resonance, and calculating average bond order in a resonance hybrid
questions.question: In ozone both O–O bonds are 128 pm long, between the O–O single bond (148 pm) and the O=O double bond (121 pm). In the carbonate ion all three C–O bonds are equal. Which interpretation, with the bond order of C–O in CO₃²⁻, is correct?
