options: A) Ozone alternates rapidly between two forms, each with one single and one double bond; C–O bond order in CO₃²⁻ is 2
B) Ozone has two double bonds; C–O bond order is 1
C) The bonds are equal because each oxygen is sp³ hybridised; C–O bond order is 3/2

D) The real molecule is a resonance hybrid of the canonical structures, none of which alone represents it; the electrons are delocalised so the two O–O bonds in O₃ are identical and intermediate between single and double (bond order 1.5); in CO₃²⁻ three equivalent structures each have one C=O and two C–O⁻, so the average bond order is (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 4/3 ≈ 1.33; resonance stabilises the molecule, and the energy difference between the hybrid and the most stable canonical form is the resonance energy
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Resonance hybrid; O–O bond order 1.5 in O₃; C–O bond order 4/3 in CO₃²⁻.
Concept: It is often observed that a single Lewis structure is inadequate for the representation of a molecule in conformity with its experimentally determined parameters; for example, the ozone molecule can be equally represented by two structures, each with one O–O single bond and one O=O double bond. Experimentally determined oxygen–oxygen bond lengths in the O₃ molecule are the same (128 pm); thus the oxygen–oxygen bonds in the O₃ molecule are intermediate between a double and a single bond, since the normal O–O and O=O bond lengths are 148 pm and 121 pm respectively. According to the concept of resonance, whenever a single Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule accurately, a number of structures with similar energy, positions of nuclei, bonding and non-bonding pairs of electrons are taken as the canonical structures of the hybrid which describes the molecule accurately. Resonance stabilises the molecule, as the energy of the resonance hybrid is less than the energy of any single canonical structure; the difference in energy between the actual structure and the lowest energy resonance structure is called the resonance stabilisation energy or simply the resonance energy. The canonical forms have no real existence; the molecule does not exist for a certain fraction of time in one canonical form and for other fractions in other canonical forms. The single Lewis structure of CO₃²⁻ based on one double bond and two single bonds cannot explain the experimental finding of all carbon–oxygen bonds being equivalent; therefore the carbonate ion is best described as a resonance hybrid of three canonical forms.
Given: O₃: 128 pm (single 148, double 121); CO₃²⁻: three equal C–O bonds.
Formula/Principle: Average bond order = total bonds between the central atom and the ligands ÷ number of equivalent positions.
Step 1: O₃: one single + one double over two positions ⇒ (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5.
Step 2: CO₃²⁻: one double + two single over three positions ⇒ (2 + 1 + 1)/3 = 4/3.
Step 3: Intermediate bond order ⇒ intermediate bond length, matching 128 pm.
Why: Delocalisation spreads the π electrons equally over all equivalent bonds, so the bonds have identical lengths.
Why not the others: (A) Canonical forms do not interconvert; bond order is 4/3. (B) Wrong structures. (C) Hybridisation does not explain it; the bond order is not 3/2.
Key point: Resonance hybrid: equal bonds; O₃ bond order 1.5, CO₃²⁻ 4/3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Explaining the bond angles of NO₂⁺, NO₂ and NO₂⁻ and of NH₃ and PH₃ by VSEPR theory and the effect of lone pairs and electronegativity
questions.question: Observed bond angles are NO₂⁺ 180°, NO₂ about 134°, NO₂⁻ about 115°, NH₃ 107° and PH₃ 93.6°. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) NO₂⁺ has no non-bonding electrons on N and is linear; NO₂ has one unpaired electron and NO₂⁻ a full lone pair on N, and since repulsion decreases in the order lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair, a lone pair compresses the angle more than a single electron does; in NH₃ the bond pairs lie closer to the more electronegative N, so bond-pair repulsion is greater and the angle is larger than in PH₃, where the bonding pairs are farther from the larger, less electronegative P
B) NO₂⁻ has the largest angle because it carries the most electrons
C) NH₃ and PH₃ have the same angle since both have one lone pair
D) NO₂⁺ is bent because N has a lone pair
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) NO₂⁺ linear (no lone electrons); one electron in NO₂ repels less than a lone pair in NO₂⁻; NH₃ > PH₃ due to electronegativity and size.
Concept: The Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion (VSEPR) theory states: the shape of a molecule depends upon the number of valence shell electron pairs (bonded or non-bonded) around the central atom; pairs of electrons in the valence shell repel one another since their electron clouds are negatively charged; these pairs tend to occupy such positions in space that minimise repulsion and thus maximise distance between them. The lone pairs are localised on the central atom, while each bonded pair is shared between two atoms; as a result, the lone pair electrons in a molecule occupy more space as compared to the bonding pairs of electrons, which results in greater repulsion between lone pairs as compared to the lone pair–bond pair and bond pair–bond pair repulsions; the descending order is lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp. Nyholm and Gillespie (1957) refined the VSEPR model by explaining the important difference between lone pairs and bonding pairs of electrons. In NO₂⁺ the nitrogen has two σ and two π bonds and no non-bonding electrons, so it is linear (180°). NO₂ has a single unpaired electron on N, which repels less than a full pair, so the angle opens to about 134°, while NO₂⁻ has a full lone pair and closes to about 115°. In hydrides of group 15, as the central atom becomes larger and less electronegative, the bonding pairs move away from it; bond-pair repulsion falls and the lone pair dominates, so the angle falls from NH₃ (107°) to PH₃ (93.6°).
Why: The more electron density sits on the central atom as non-bonding electrons, and the farther the bonding pairs are from it, the smaller the bond angle.
Why not the others: (B) More non-bonding density gives a smaller angle. (C) Electronegativity and size of the central atom differ. (D) NO₂⁺ has no lone pair on N and is linear.
Key point: Angle ↓ with more non-bonding electrons on the central atom: NO₂⁺ > NO₂ > NO₂⁻; NH₃ > PH₃.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating reaction enthalpy for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl from bond enthalpies, and comparing fuels by enthalpy of combustion per gram
questions.question: Bond enthalpies: H–H 435, Cl–Cl 243, H–Cl 431 kJ mol⁻¹. Standard enthalpies of combustion: H₂ −286, CH₄ −890 and C(graphite) −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔrH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g), and what is the order of the fuels by heat released per gram?
options: A) −184 kJ; C > CH₄ > H₂
B) +184 kJ; H₂ > CH₄ > C
C) −184 kJ; H₂ (≈143 kJ g⁻¹) > CH₄ (≈55.6 kJ g⁻¹) > C (≈32.8 kJ g⁻¹)
D) −431 kJ; CH₄ > H₂ > C
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ΔrH = −184 kJ; per gram H₂ 143 > CH₄ 55.6 > C 32.8 kJ.
Concept: For gaseous reactions, the standard enthalpy of reaction can be estimated from bond enthalpies: ΔrH° = Σ bond enthalpies of reactants − Σ bond enthalpies of products, since energy is required to break bonds and released when bonds are formed. This relationship is approximate and valid when all substances (reactants and products) in the reaction are in the gaseous state. The standard enthalpy of combustion is the enthalpy change per mole (or per unit amount) of a substance when it undergoes combustion and all the reactants and products are in their standard states; cooking gas in cylinders contains mostly butane, and enthalpies of combustion are used to compare fuels. Dividing the molar enthalpy of combustion by the molar mass gives the heat released per gram (the calorific value), which decides which fuel delivers most energy for a given mass.
Given: Bond enthalpies; ΔcH°: H₂ −286, CH₄ −890, C −393.5 kJ mol⁻¹; M = 2, 16, 12 g mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: ΔrH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed); heat per gram = |ΔcH|/M.
Step 1: Bonds broken: 435 + 243 = 678 kJ; bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ.
Step 2: ΔrH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ.
Step 3: Per gram: 286/2 = 143; 890/16 = 55.6; 393.5/12 = 32.8 kJ g⁻¹ ⇒ H₂ > CH₄ > C.
Why: Stronger bonds formed than broken make the reaction exothermic; hydrogen's very low molar mass gives it the highest energy per gram.
Why not the others: (A) Per-gram order reversed. (B) Sign wrong. (D) Counts only one H–Cl bond.
Key point: ΔrH = bonds broken − bonds formed; H₂ has the highest calorific value per gram.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using ΔH and ΔS to decide the spontaneity of an endothermic dissolution and the temperature at which ΔG changes sign
questions.question: For NH₄NO₃(s) → NH₄⁺(aq) + NO₃⁻(aq), ΔH° = +25.7 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS° = +108.7 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. What is ΔG° at 298 K, and below what temperature would dissolution become non-spontaneous (assuming ΔH and ΔS constant)?
options: A) +6.7 kJ; above 236 K
B) −6.7 kJ; below about 236 K
C) −32.4 kJ; below 100 K
D) +25.7 kJ; it is never spontaneous
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) ΔG° ≈ −6.7 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K; non-spontaneous below about 236 K.
Concept: The Gibbs energy change ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is the criterion of spontaneity at constant temperature and pressure: if ΔG is negative the process is spontaneous, if positive it is non-spontaneous. For an endothermic process (ΔH positive) to be spontaneous, ΔS must be positive and TΔS must exceed ΔH, so such processes become spontaneous only at sufficiently high temperature. The dissolution of ammonium nitrate absorbs heat (the solution becomes cold, which is used in instant cold packs) yet occurs spontaneously at room temperature, because the large increase in disorder as the ordered ionic lattice breaks into mobile hydrated ions makes TΔS larger than ΔH. The temperature at which ΔG = 0 is T = ΔH/ΔS; above it the process is spontaneous and below it non-spontaneous.
Given: ΔH = 25.7 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = 0.1087 kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T = 298 K.
Formula/Principle: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; crossover T = ΔH/ΔS.
Step 1: TΔS = 298 × 0.1087 = 32.4 kJ.
Step 2: ΔG = 25.7 − 32.4 = −6.7 kJ mol⁻¹ ⇒ spontaneous.
Step 3: T = 25.7/0.1087 ≈ 236 K ⇒ non-spontaneous below about 236 K.
Why: The entropy term grows with temperature; at room temperature it outweighs the endothermic enthalpy term.
Why not the others: (A) Sign of ΔG wrong and direction reversed. (C) Gives only −TΔS. (D) Ignores the entropy term.
Key point: Endothermic + ΔS > 0 ⇒ spontaneous above T = ΔH/ΔS.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the hydrolysis constant and pH of a salt of a weak base and strong acid, and predicting whether other salt solutions are acidic or basic
questions.question: For NH₃, Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ and Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴. What is the hydrolysis constant of NH₄⁺ and the pH of 0.01 M NH₄Cl, and which statement about other salts is correct?
options: A) Kh = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹; pH 8.37; Na₂CO₃ solution is acidic

B) Kh = Kw/Kb ≈ 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰; [H⁺] = √(Kh·c) ≈ 2.36 × 10⁻⁶ M, so pH ≈ 5.63; Na₂CO₃ (salt of a weak acid and strong base) gives a basic solution, and FeCl₃ (salt of a weak base and strong acid) an acidic one; NaCl solution is neutral
C) Kh = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰; pH 7.00 because NH₄Cl is a salt
D) Kh = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵; pH 3.37; FeCl₃ solution is basic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Kh ≈ 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰; pH ≈ 5.63; Na₂CO₃ basic, FeCl₃ acidic, NaCl neutral.
Concept: The cations (e.g. Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Ba²⁺) of strong bases and anions (e.g. Cl⁻, Br⁻, NO₃⁻, ClO₄⁻) of strong acids simply get hydrated but do not hydrolyse, and therefore solutions of salts formed from strong acids and bases are neutral (pH 7). The other category of salts do undergo hydrolysis. Salts of weak acid and strong base, e.g. CH₃COONa or Na₂CO₃, give basic solutions because the anion takes a proton from water, releasing OH⁻. Similarly NH₄Cl, formed from a weak base NH₄OH and strong acid HCl, in water dissociates completely; ammonium ions undergo hydrolysis with water to form NH₄OH and H⁺ ions, and the solution becomes acidic. For the conjugate acid of a weak base, Kh = Kw/Kb; with a small degree of hydrolysis, [H⁺] = √(Kh·c).
Given: Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, c = 0.01 M.
Formula/Principle: Kh = Kw/Kb; [H⁺] = √(Kh·c); pH = −log[H⁺].
Step 1: Kh = 10⁻¹⁴/1.8 × 10⁻⁵ = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰.
Step 2: [H⁺] = √(5.56 × 10⁻¹⁰ × 0.01) = √(5.56 × 10⁻¹²) = 2.36 × 10⁻⁶ M.
Step 3: pH = 6 − log 2.36 = 6 − 0.37 = 5.63.
Why: NH₄⁺ is a weak acid, so its hydrolysis releases a little H⁺, making the solution mildly acidic.
Why not the others: (A) Kh wrong, pH on the wrong side; Na₂CO₃ is basic. (C) Ignores cation hydrolysis. (D) Uses Kb as Kh; FeCl₃ is acidic.
Key point: Salt of weak base + strong acid: Kh = Kw/Kb, acidic; NH₄Cl 0.01 M ⇒ pH ≈ 5.6.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the percentage of a halogen by the Carius method from the mass of silver halide, and the analogous estimation of sulphur as barium sulphate
questions.question: In a Carius estimation, 0.15 g of an organic compound gave 0.12 g of silver bromide. In another estimation, 0.16 g of a compound gave 0.233 g of barium sulphate. (Ag = 108, Br = 80, Ba = 137, S = 32, O = 16.) What are the percentages of bromine and of sulphur?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Br ≈ 34.0 %; S = 20.0 %.
Concept: In the Carius method for halogens, a known mass of an organic compound is heated with fuming nitric acid in the presence of silver nitrate contained in a hard glass tube known as a Carius tube, in a furnace; carbon and hydrogen present in the compound are oxidised to carbon dioxide and water, and the halogen present forms the corresponding silver halide (AgX), which is filtered, washed, dried and weighed. Let the mass of organic compound taken be m g and the mass of AgX formed be m₁ g; 1 mol of AgX contains 1 mol of X, so mass of halogen in m₁ g of AgX = (atomic mass of X × m₁)/(molecular mass of AgX), and percentage of halogen = (atomic mass of X × m₁ × 100)/(molecular mass of AgX × m). For sulphur, a known mass of an organic compound is heated in a Carius tube with sodium peroxide or fuming nitric acid; sulphur present in the compound is oxidised to sulphuric acid, which is precipitated as barium sulphate by adding excess of barium chloride solution in water; the precipitate is filtered, washed, dried and weighed, and the percentage of sulphur = (32 × m₁ × 100)/(233 × m).
Given: m = 0.15 g, m(AgBr) = 0.12 g, M(AgBr) = 188; m = 0.16 g, m(BaSO₄) = 0.233 g, M(BaSO₄) = 233.
Formula/Principle: %X = (A(X)/M(AgX)) × (m₁/m) × 100; %S = (32/233) × (m₁/m) × 100.
Step 1: Br in AgBr = 0.12 × 80/188 = 0.0511 g.
Step 2: %Br = 0.0511/0.15 × 100 = 34.0 %.
Step 3: %S = (32/233) × (0.233/0.16) × 100 = 0.032/0.16 × 100 = 20.0 %.
Why: Each mole of precipitate carries exactly one mole of the element being estimated, so its mass fraction in the precipitate converts precipitate mass into element mass.
Why not the others: (A) Uses precipitate mass ratios without the element fraction. (B) Wrong fractions. (C) Arithmetic errors in both.
Key point: Carius: %X = (A_X/M_AgX)(m₁/m)×100; %S = (32/233)(m₁/m)×100.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking substituted benzenes by rate of nitration using activating and deactivating effects, and the mechanism of nitration through the nitronium ion and σ-complex
questions.question: Which order of rate of nitration, with its explanation, is correct?
options: A) Nitrobenzene > chlorobenzene > benzene > toluene > phenol, because electron-withdrawing groups attract the electrophile
B) All monosubstituted benzenes nitrate at the same rate, since the ring is aromatic in each case

C) Phenol > toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene: –OH (+R) and –CH₃ (+I, hyperconjugation) increase electron density in the ring and activate it, while –Cl (−I > +R) and –NO₂ (−R, −I) deactivate it; in nitration, HNO₃ is protonated by H₂SO₄ and loses water to give the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, which attacks the ring in the slow step to form a resonance-stabilised arenium ion (σ-complex), and loss of a proton to HSO₄⁻ restores aromaticity
D) Toluene > phenol > benzene > nitrobenzene > chlorobenzene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Phenol > toluene > benzene > chlorobenzene > nitrobenzene; NO₂⁺ electrophile; σ-complex formation is slow; deprotonation restores aromaticity.
Concept: Aromatic compounds undergo electrophilic substitution reactions, and the mechanism involves three steps: (a) generation of the electrophile, (b) formation of carbocation intermediate, (c) removal of proton from the carbocation intermediate. In nitration, the electrophile is the nitronium ion NO₂⁺, produced by transfer of a proton from sulphuric acid to nitric acid: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ ⇌ NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. The electrophile attacks the aromatic ring to form a carbocation (arenium ion or σ-complex), in which one carbon is sp³ hybridised; the arenium ion is stabilised by resonance; finally the sigma complex releases a proton from the sp³ carbon on attack by HSO₄⁻ and the aromatic character is restored. Groups which increase the electron density of the benzene ring by +R or +I effects (–OH, –NH₂, –OR, –CH₃) are activating groups and make substitution faster than in benzene; groups such as –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH withdraw electrons by −R and −I effects and deactivate the ring; halogens are deactivating because their strong −I effect outweighs their +R effect, though they are ortho and para directing.
Step 1: –OH (strong +R) > –CH₃ (+I, hyperconjugation) > H ⇒ phenol > toluene > benzene.
Step 2: –Cl (−I > +R) mildly deactivating ⇒ chlorobenzene below benzene.
Step 3: –NO₂ (strong −R, −I) ⇒ nitrobenzene slowest.
Why: The slow step is attack by the electrophile; a richer π cloud attracts NO₂⁺ more and better stabilises the arenium ion.
Why not the others: (A) Order reversed. (B) Substituents strongly affect rate. (D) Phenol is more activated than toluene, and nitrobenzene is slower than chlorobenzene.
Key point: Rate of nitration: phenol > toluene > benzene > PhCl > PhNO₂.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting the products of nitrating toluene, nitrobenzene and chlorobenzene in terms of ortho/para and meta directing groups
questions.question: Nitration under similar conditions gives: toluene → mainly 2- and 4-nitrotoluene, faster than benzene; nitrobenzene → mainly 1,3-dinitrobenzene, slowly and only at higher temperature; chlorobenzene → mainly 1-chloro-2-nitro- and 1-chloro-4-nitrobenzene, slower than benzene. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) –CH₃ is ortho/para directing and activating; –NO₂ is meta directing and deactivating, because its −R effect withdraws electron density mainly from the ortho and para positions, leaving the meta position relatively richer; –Cl is ortho/para directing (its +R effect raises density at ortho and para) but deactivating (its strong −I effect lowers overall density), so chlorobenzene nitrates more slowly than benzene yet gives o- and p-products
B) –Cl is meta directing because it is electronegative
C) –NO₂ is ortho/para directing and activating
D) All three groups are meta directing because they are attached directly to the ring
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) –CH₃ o/p and activating; –NO₂ meta and deactivating; –Cl o/p but deactivating.
Concept: When monosubstituted benzene is subjected to further substitution, three possible disubstituted products are not formed in equal amounts; two types of behaviour are observed — either ortho and para products or meta product are predominantly formed; this behaviour depends on the nature of the substituent already present in the benzene ring, and is known as the directive influence of substituents. Ortho and para directing groups: the groups which direct the incoming group to ortho and para positions; examples are –NH₂, –NHR, –NHCOCH₃, –OCH₃, –CH₃, –C₂H₅; generally these groups activate the ring. Meta directing groups: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO₃H; these withdraw electrons from the ring by resonance (−R), and the electron density at ortho and para positions falls more than at meta, so the electrophile attacks the meta position; they also deactivate the ring. In the case of aryl halides, halogens are moderately deactivating; because of their strong −I effect, the overall electron density on the benzene ring decreases; however, due to resonance the electron density on ortho and para positions is greater than that at the meta position, hence they are also ortho and para directing groups.
Step 1: Toluene: o/p products, faster than benzene ⇒ activating o/p director.
Step 2: Nitrobenzene: meta product, slow ⇒ deactivating meta director.
Step 3: Chlorobenzene: o/p products, slower than benzene ⇒ deactivating o/p director.
Why: The orientation depends on where electron density (and stabilisation of the arenium ion) is greatest; the rate depends on overall ring density.
Why not the others: (B) Halogens are o/p directors. (C) –NO₂ is meta directing and deactivating. (D) The groups behave differently.
Key point: –CH₃ o/p activating; –NO₂ meta deactivating; –Cl o/p deactivating.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using the van't Hoff factor to find the degree of association of acetic acid in benzene and the degree of dissociation of NaCl from freezing-point depression
questions.question: Acetic acid (M = 60) dissolved in benzene shows an apparent molar mass of 105 by freezing-point depression. A 0.1 m aqueous NaCl solution freezes at −0.348 °C (Kf of water = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹). What is the degree of association of acetic acid and the degree of dissociation of NaCl?
options: A) Acetic acid 85.7 % associated (dimers formed by hydrogen bonding, i = 0.571); NaCl 87 % dissociated (i = 1.87)
B) Acetic acid 57.1 % associated; NaCl 100 % dissociated
C) Acetic acid 42.9 % associated; NaCl 74 % dissociated
D) Acetic acid 100 % associated; NaCl 87 % dissociated
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) i = 0.571, 85.7 % association; i = 1.87, 87 % dissociation.
Concept: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles; when solute particles associate or dissociate in solution, the observed colligative property differs from that calculated, and the molar mass so determined is called the abnormal molar mass. In 1880 van't Hoff introduced a factor i, known as the van't Hoff factor, to account for the extent of dissociation or association: i = normal molar mass/abnormal molar mass = observed colligative property/calculated colligative property. In the case of association, the value of i is less than unity, while for dissociation it is greater than unity. For example, ethanoic acid (acetic acid) dimerises in benzene due to hydrogen bonding, while in water KCl and NaCl dissociate into ions. For association of n molecules into one, i = 1 − α(1 − 1/n); for dissociation into ν ions, i = 1 + α(ν − 1).
Given: M(normal) = 60, M(observed) = 105; ΔTf = 0.348 K, m = 0.1, Kf = 1.86.
Formula/Principle: i = M_normal/M_observed; association into dimers: i = 1 − α/2; ΔTf = iKf m; dissociation: i = 1 + α.
Step 1: i = 60/105 = 0.571 ⇒ α/2 = 0.429 ⇒ α = 0.857 (85.7 %).
Step 2: NaCl: i = 0.348/(1.86 × 0.1) = 1.87.
Step 3: i = 1 + α ⇒ α = 0.87 (87 %).
Why: Association reduces the number of particles and dissociation increases it, so i < 1 for the dimerising acid and i > 1 for the ionising salt.
Why not the others: (B) Takes i itself as the degree of association, and full dissociation ignores the data. (C) Takes 1 − i as α. (D) Complete association would give M = 120.
Key point: i = normal/observed molar mass; dimer α = 2(1 − i); salt α = i − 1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating ΔG° and the equilibrium constant of a Cu–Ag galvanic cell from its standard EMF
questions.question: For the cell Cu(s) | Cu²⁺(aq) || Ag⁺(aq) | Ag(s), E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V and E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V. What are E°cell, ΔrG° and log K for Cu + 2Ag⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Ag at 298 K? (F = 96 500 C mol⁻¹)
options: C) E° = 0.46 V; ΔG° = −nFE° = −2 × 96 500 × 0.46 ≈ −88.8 kJ mol⁻¹; log K = nE°/0.059 = 2 × 0.46/0.059 ≈ 15.6, so K ≈ 4 × 10¹⁵ and the reaction goes essentially to completion
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) E° = 0.46 V; ΔG° ≈ −88.8 kJ mol⁻¹; log K ≈ 15.6.
Concept: The potential of a cell is the difference between the electrode potentials (reduction potentials) of the cathode and anode: E°cell = E°right − E°left = E°cathode − E°anode. Electrical work done in one second is equal to the electrical potential multiplied by the total charge passed; if we want to obtain maximum work from a galvanic cell then charge has to be passed reversibly, and the reversible work done by a galvanic cell is equal to the decrease in its Gibbs energy: ΔrG° = −nFE°cell, where n is the number of moles of electrons. At equilibrium, ΔrG° = −RT ln K, so E°cell = (2.303RT/nF) log K = (0.059/n) log K at 298 K. A positive E° means a negative ΔG° and K > 1.
Given: E°cathode (Ag) = 0.80 V, E°anode (Cu) = 0.34 V, n = 2.
Formula/Principle: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.059.
Step 1: E°cell = 0.80 − 0.34 = 0.46 V.
Step 2: ΔG° = −2 × 96 500 × 0.46 = −88 780 J ≈ −88.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
Step 3: log K = 2 × 0.46/0.059 = 15.6.
Why: Two electrons are transferred per Cu atom, and a sizeable positive E° gives a very large equilibrium constant.
Why not the others: (A) Adds the potentials. (B) Uses n = 1. (D) Reverses cathode and anode.
Key point: ΔG° = −nFE°; log K = nE°/0.059 at 298 K.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating activation energy from rate constants at two temperatures using the Arrhenius equation
questions.question: The rate constant of a reaction triples when the temperature is raised from 300 K to 320 K. What is the activation energy? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, log 3 = 0.477)
options: A) 22.0 kJ mol⁻¹
B) 43.9 kJ mol⁻¹
C) 87.8 kJ mol⁻¹
D) 4.39 kJ mol⁻¹
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ea ≈ 43.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Concept: Most of the chemical reactions are accelerated by increase in temperature; for example, in decomposition of N₂O₅ the time taken for half of the original amount of material to decompose is 12 min at 50 °C, 5 h at 25 °C and 10 days at 0 °C. The temperature dependence of the rate of a chemical reaction can be accurately explained by the Arrhenius equation, k = A e^(−Ea/RT), where A is the Arrhenius factor or frequency factor, R the gas constant and Ea the activation energy measured in joules/mole. Taking logarithms at two temperatures and subtracting gives log(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/2.303R)[(T₂ − T₁)/(T₁T₂)], which allows Ea to be found from rate constants at two temperatures.
Given: k₂/k₁ = 3, T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 320 K.
Formula/Principle: log(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/2.303R)·(T₂ − T₁)/(T₁T₂).
Step 1: (T₂ − T₁)/(T₁T₂) = 20/96 000 = 2.083 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹.
Step 2: 0.477 = Ea × 2.083 × 10⁻⁴/(2.303 × 8.314) = Ea × 1.088 × 10⁻⁵.
Step 3: Ea = 0.477/1.088 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 43 850 J ≈ 43.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why: A modest 20 K rise tripling k indicates a moderate barrier; a larger Ea would make k far more sensitive to temperature.
Why not the others: (A) Halved. (C) Doubled. (D) Off by a factor of 10.
Key point: log(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/2.303R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Calculating how much a catalyst increases the rate by lowering the activation energy, and why ΔH and the equilibrium constant are unchanged
questions.question: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of a reaction from 100 kJ mol⁻¹ to 75 kJ mol⁻¹ at 300 K, with the Arrhenius factor unchanged. By about what factor does the rate increase, and what happens to ΔH and K?
options: A) About 25 times; ΔH falls by 25 kJ
B) About 10 times; K increases
C) About 1.33 times; ΔH and K unchanged

D) About e^(25 000/(8.314 × 300)) = e^10.02 ≈ 2.2 × 10⁴ times; ΔH and the equilibrium constant are unchanged, because the catalyst lowers the barrier for the forward and reverse reactions equally and only helps equilibrium to be reached sooner
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Rate increases about 2.2 × 10⁴ times; ΔH and K unchanged.
Concept: A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a reaction without itself undergoing any permanent chemical change. According to intermediate complex theory, a catalyst participates in a chemical reaction by forming temporary bonds with the reactants, resulting in an intermediate complex, which has a transitory existence and decomposes to yield products and the catalyst. It is believed that the catalyst provides an alternate pathway or reaction mechanism by reducing the activation energy between reactants and products and hence lowering the potential energy barrier. It is clear from the Arrhenius equation that the lower the value of activation energy, the faster will be the rate of a reaction. A small amount of the catalyst can catalyse a large amount of reactants; a catalyst does not alter Gibbs energy, ΔG, of a reaction; it catalyses the spontaneous reactions but does not catalyse non-spontaneous reactions; it is also found that a catalyst does not change the equilibrium constant of a reaction, rather it helps in attaining the equilibrium faster, that is, it catalyses the forward as well as the backward reactions to the same extent so that the equilibrium state remains the same but is reached earlier.
Given: Ea = 100 → 75 kJ mol⁻¹, T = 300 K, A unchanged.
Formula/Principle: k_cat/k = e^((Ea − Ea,cat)/RT).
Step 1: ΔEa = 25 000 J mol⁻¹; RT = 8.314 × 300 = 2494 J mol⁻¹.
Step 2: Exponent = 25 000/2494 = 10.02.
Step 3: e^10.02 ≈ 2.2 × 10⁴.
Why: The rate depends exponentially on Ea/RT, so a modest drop in barrier gives an enormous rate increase, while reactant and product energies are unaffected.
Why not the others: (A) Treats rate as proportional to ΔEa and wrongly changes ΔH. (B) Factor wrong; K unchanged. (C) Uses the ratio of activation energies.
Key point: Rate ratio = e^(ΔEa/RT); catalysts leave ΔH, ΔG and K unchanged.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting data on lanthanoid ionic radii, the oxidising power of Ce⁴⁺ and reducing power of Eu²⁺, and the trend in basicity of Ln(OH)₃
questions.question: Data: ionic radii fall steadily from La³⁺ (103 pm) to Lu³⁺ (86 pm); E°(Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺) = +1.74 V; Eu²⁺ is readily oxidised to Eu³⁺. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The steady decrease is the lanthanoid contraction, caused by the imperfect shielding of one 4f electron by another as nuclear charge increases; Ce⁴⁺ (favoured by its noble-gas configuration) is a strong oxidant that reverts to the common +3 state, while Eu²⁺ (4f⁷) is a strong reducing agent that changes to +3; because the cation size decreases, covalent character of Ln–OH bonds increases and the basicity of the hydroxides decreases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃
B) The radii decrease because the 4f electrons shield the outer electrons very effectively
C) Ce⁴⁺ is a reducing agent and Eu²⁺ an oxidising agent
D) The basicity of the hydroxides increases from La(OH)₃ to Lu(OH)₃
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lanthanoid contraction from poor 4f shielding; Ce⁴⁺ oxidant, Eu²⁺ reductant; basicity of Ln(OH)₃ decreases across the series.
Concept: The overall decrease in atomic and ionic radii from lanthanum to lutetium (the lanthanoid contraction) is a unique feature in the chemistry of the lanthanoids; it has far-reaching consequences in the chemistry of the third transition series of the elements. The decrease in atomic radii (derived from the structures of metals) is not quite regular as it is regular in M³⁺ ions. The cause of the lanthanoid contraction is the imperfect shielding of one electron by another in the same set of orbitals; the shielding of one 4f electron by another is less than that of one d electron by another with the increase in nuclear charge along the series. In the lanthanoids, La(II) and La(III) compounds are predominant; however, occasionally +2 and +4 ions in solution or in solid compounds are also obtained; this irregularity arises mainly from the extra stability of empty, half-filled or filled f subshell. Thus the formation of Ce⁴⁺ is favoured by its noble gas configuration, but it is a strong oxidant reverting to the common +3 state; the E° value for Ce⁴⁺/Ce³⁺ is +1.74 V, which suggests that it can oxidise water; however, the reaction rate is very slow and hence Ce(IV) is a good analytical reagent. Eu²⁺ is formed by losing the two s electrons, and its f⁷ configuration accounts for the formation of this ion; however, Eu²⁺ is a strong reducing agent changing to the common +3 state. Lanthanoid hydroxides Ln(OH)₃ are basic like alkaline earth metal hydroxides, and their basicity decreases with increasing atomic number as covalent character increases with decreasing ionic size.
Why: Size controls charge density: smaller Ln³⁺ ions polarise the hydroxide more, so the M–OH bond becomes more covalent and less basic.
Why not the others: (B) 4f electrons shield poorly. (C) Roles reversed. (D) Basicity decreases across the series.
Key point: Lanthanoid contraction (poor 4f shielding); Ce⁴⁺ oxidant, Eu²⁺ reductant; Ln(OH)₃ basicity ↓.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the actinoids with the lanthanoids — range of oxidation states, contraction, radioactivity and magnetic behaviour — and the reasons for the differences
questions.question: Which comparison of actinoids with lanthanoids is correct?
options: A) Lanthanoids show a wider range of oxidation states than actinoids because 4f orbitals are more exposed

B) Actinoids show a greater range of oxidation states (e.g. Np and Pu up to +7), because 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies; the actinoid contraction from element to element is greater than the lanthanoid contraction, owing to poorer shielding by 5f electrons; all actinoids are radioactive, many with short half-lives, which makes their study difficult; and their magnetic properties are more complex than those of the lanthanoids
C) The actinoid contraction is smaller than the lanthanoid contraction because 5f electrons shield better
D) Actinoids are less reactive than lanthanoids and none of them is radioactive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Wider oxidation states (to +7), greater contraction, radioactivity, more complex magnetism in actinoids.
Concept: The actinoids include the fourteen elements from Th to Lr; they are radioactive elements, and the earlier members have relatively long half-lives while the latter ones have half-life values ranging from a day to 3 minutes for lawrencium (Z = 103); the latter members could be prepared only in nanogram quantities; these facts render their study more difficult. There is a gradual decrease in the size of atoms or M³⁺ ions across the series; this may be referred to as the actinoid contraction (like the lanthanoid contraction); the contraction is, however, greater from element to element in this series resulting from poor shielding by 5f electrons. There is a greater range of oxidation states, which is in part attributed to the fact that the 5f, 6d and 7s levels are of comparable energies; the known oxidation states of actinoids show that the elements in the first half of the series frequently exhibit higher oxidation states; for example, the maximum oxidation state increases from +4 in Th to +5, +6 and +7 respectively in Pa, U and Np, but decreases in succeeding elements. The actinoid metals are all silvery in appearance but display a variety of structures; they are highly reactive metals, especially when finely divided. The magnetic properties of the actinoids are more complex than those of the lanthanoids, although the variation in the magnetic susceptibility of the actinoids with the number of unpaired 5f electrons is roughly parallel to the corresponding results for the lanthanoids.
Why: The 5f orbitals extend further out and lie closer in energy to 6d and 7s than 4f does to 5d and 6s, so more electrons can take part in bonding.
Why not the others: (A) Actinoids have the wider range. (C) The actinoid contraction is greater. (D) Actinoids are highly reactive and all radioactive.
Key point: Actinoids: more oxidation states, greater contraction, all radioactive, complex magnetism.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Predicting hybridisation, number of unpaired electrons and spin-only magnetic moments of Mn, Ni and Co complexes by valence bond theory
questions.question: Using valence bond theory, which set of predictions is correct for [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻, [MnCl₄]²⁻, [Ni(CO)₄] and [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻?
options: A) [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻ sp³d², 4 unpaired; [MnCl₄]²⁻ dsp², 1 unpaired
B) [Ni(CO)₄] dsp², paramagnetic with 2 unpaired electrons
C) [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ sp³d², 4 unpaired, μ = 4.90 BM

D) [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻: Mn³⁺ (3d⁴) with strong-field CN⁻ pairs into three orbitals, d²sp³, 2 unpaired, μ = √8 ≈ 2.83 BM; [MnCl₄]²⁻: Mn²⁺ (3d⁵), sp³ tetrahedral, 5 unpaired, μ = √35 ≈ 5.92 BM; [Ni(CO)₄]: Ni(0) 3d¹⁰, sp³ tetrahedral, diamagnetic; [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻: Co³⁺ (3d⁶) with oxalate pairing, d²sp³, diamagnetic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻ d²sp³, 2.83 BM; [MnCl₄]²⁻ sp³, 5.92 BM; [Ni(CO)₄] sp³, diamagnetic; [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻ d²sp³, diamagnetic.
Concept: According to valence bond theory, the metal atom or ion under the influence of ligands can use its (n−1)d, ns, np or ns, np, nd orbitals for hybridisation to yield a set of equivalent orbitals of definite geometry such as octahedral, tetrahedral or square planar; these hybridised orbitals are allowed to overlap with ligand orbitals that can donate electron pairs for bonding. In octahedral complexes, a complex that uses inner d orbitals (n−1)d for hybridisation (d²sp³) is called an inner orbital or low spin or spin paired complex; a complex that uses outer nd orbitals (sp³d²) is called an outer orbital or high spin or spin free complex. Strong-field ligands such as CN⁻, CO and (often) C₂O₄²⁻ with Co³⁺ cause pairing; weak-field ligands such as Cl⁻ do not. The spin-only magnetic moment is μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
Given: Mn³⁺ d⁴, Mn²⁺ d⁵, Ni(0) d⁸4s² → d¹⁰ with CO, Co³⁺ d⁶.
Formula/Principle: μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM.
Step 1: [Mn(CN)₆]³⁻: d⁴ paired into 3 orbitals ⇒ 2 unpaired, two 3d free ⇒ d²sp³; μ = √8 = 2.83 BM.
Step 2: [MnCl₄]²⁻: d⁵ unpaired, weak field, sp³ ⇒ μ = √35 = 5.92 BM.
Step 3: [Ni(CO)₄]: d¹⁰ ⇒ sp³, n = 0; [Co(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻: d⁶ paired ⇒ d²sp³, n = 0.
Why: Strong-field ligands force pairing to free inner d orbitals, giving low-spin inner orbital complexes; weak-field ligands leave electrons unpaired.
Why not the others: (A) Wrong hybridisations and electron counts. (B) [Ni(CO)₄] is tetrahedral and diamagnetic. (C) Oxalate pairs the d⁶ electrons of Co³⁺ here.
Key point: Strong field → pairing → inner orbital (d²sp³); μ = √(n(n+2)).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Using crystal field theory to decide high- or low-spin configurations from Δo and pairing energy, why tetrahedral complexes are high spin, and the origin of colour in hydrated copper sulphate
questions.question: Which explanation based on crystal field theory is correct?
options: A) For a d⁴ ion, the fourth electron always enters the t₂g set, whatever the ligand
B) Tetrahedral complexes are usually low spin because Δt is larger than Δo

C) For d⁴ in an octahedral field, if Δo < P (pairing energy) the fourth electron enters an eg orbital giving t₂g³eg¹ (high spin, weak-field ligands), and if Δo > P it pairs in t₂g giving t₂g⁴eg⁰ (low spin, strong-field ligands); Δt ≈ (4/9)Δo, so orbital splitting energies are usually too small to force pairing and low-spin tetrahedral complexes are rarely observed; CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue because water ligands split the d levels and d–d transitions absorb visible light, while anhydrous CuSO₄, lacking water ligands, is white
D) Anhydrous CuSO₄ is blue and the hydrate is white
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Δo < P → high spin t₂g³eg¹; Δo > P → low spin t₂g⁴; Δt = (4/9)Δo so tetrahedral complexes are high spin; hydrate blue, anhydrous white.
Concept: The crystal field theory (CFT) is an electrostatic model which considers the metal–ligand bond to be ionic, arising purely from electrostatic interactions between the metal ion and the ligand. In an octahedral coordination entity with six ligands surrounding the metal atom/ion, the five d orbitals split into a lower set of three orbitals (t₂g) and a higher set of two orbitals (eg); the energy separation is denoted by Δo. For d⁴ ions, two possible patterns of electron distribution arise: (i) the fourth electron could either enter the t₂g level and pair with an existing electron, or (ii) it could avoid paying the price of the pairing energy by occupying the eg level; which of these possibilities occurs depends on the relative magnitude of the crystal field splitting Δo and the pairing energy P. If Δo < P, the fourth electron enters one of the eg orbitals, giving the configuration t₂g³eg¹; ligands for which Δo < P are known as weak field ligands and form high spin complexes. If Δo > P, it becomes more energetically favourable for the fourth electron to occupy a t₂g orbital with configuration t₂g⁴eg⁰; ligands which produce this effect are known as strong field ligands and form low spin complexes. In tetrahedral coordination entity formation the d orbital splitting is inverted and is smaller as compared to the octahedral field splitting: Δt = (4/9)Δo; consequently the orbital splitting energies are not sufficiently large for forcing pairing, and therefore low spin configurations are rarely observed. The colour of the complex is complementary to that which is absorbed; in the absence of ligands crystal field splitting does not occur and hence the substance is colourless — for example, removal of water from [Ti(H₂O)₆]Cl₃ on heating renders it colourless; similarly anhydrous CuSO₄ is white, but CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue in colour.
Why: Whether electrons pair depends on which costs less, crossing the splitting gap or pairing; colour requires d–d transitions, which need ligand-induced splitting.
Why not the others: (A) Depends on Δo versus P. (B) Δt is smaller, so tetrahedral complexes are high spin. (D) Colours reversed.
Key point: Δo vs P decides spin; Δt = (4/9)Δo ⇒ tetrahedral high spin; no ligands → no splitting → colourless.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Locating horizontal and vertical tangents and tangents of a given slope on a parametric curve, using dy/dt and dx/dt separately
questions.question: For the curve \(x=t^3-3t,\ y=t^2\), how many horizontal tangents, vertical tangents and tangents of slope \(1\) does it have, and where are the vertical tangents?
options: A) \(2\) horizontal, \(1\) vertical at \((0,0)\), \(1\) tangent of slope \(1\)
B) \(1\) horizontal, \(2\) vertical at \((0,\pm1)\), no tangent of slope \(1\)
C) \(1\) horizontal (at the origin), \(2\) vertical at \((-2,1)\) and \((2,1)\), and \(2\) tangents of slope \(1\)
D) no horizontal tangent, \(2\) vertical tangents, \(3\) tangents of slope \(1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(1\) horizontal at \((0,0)\); vertical at \((\mp2,1)\); \(2\) tangents of slope \(1\).
Given: \(x=t^3-3t,\ y=t^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dy/dt}{dx/dt};\ \text{horizontal: }\dfrac{dy}{dt}=0,\ \dfrac{dx}{dt}\ne0;\ \text{vertical: }\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0,\ \dfrac{dy}{dt}\ne0\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{dy}{dt}=2t=0\Rightarrow t=0,\ \dfrac{dx}{dt}=-3\ne0\Rightarrow\text{horizontal tangent at }(0,0)\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3t^2-3=0\Rightarrow t=\pm1;\ t=1:(-2,1),\ t=-1:(2,1)\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{2t}{3t^2-3}=1\Rightarrow3t^2-2t-3=0,\ D=4+36=40>0\Rightarrow2\text{ values of }t\)
Worked derivation: \[t=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{40}}{6}=\frac{1\pm\sqrt{10}}{3}\ne\pm1\Rightarrow\text{both give genuine tangents of slope }1\]
Check: \[t=\pm1:\ \frac{dy}{dt}=\pm2\ne0\Rightarrow\text{vertical tangents are genuine}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a parametric curve has a horizontal tangent where only }y\text{ stops changing and a vertical one where only }x\text{ stops changing}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(dy/dt\text{ vanishes only at }t=0\); (B) \(\text{vertical points are }(\mp2,1)\text{ and slope-1 tangents exist}\); (D) \(t=0\text{ gives a horizontal tangent; the quadratic has only two roots}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{\dot y}{\dot x};\ \dot y=0\to\text{horizontal},\ \dot x=0\to\text{vertical}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the point of inflection and the intervals of concavity of a cubic, and relating them to its turning points
questions.question: For \(y=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\), where is the point of inflection and on which interval is the curve concave down?
options: A) Inflection at \((2,3)\); concave down for \(x<2\), concave up for \(x>2\); local maximum \((1,5)\), local minimum \((3,1)\)
B) Inflection at \((2,3)\); concave up for \(x<2\)
C) Inflection at \((3,1)\); concave down for \(x<3\)
D) Inflection at \((1,5)\); concave down for \(x>1\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Inflection \((2,3)\); concave down on \(x<2\); max \((1,5)\), min \((3,1)\).
Given: \(y=x^3-6x^2+9x+1\)
Formula/Principle: \(y''<0\Rightarrow\text{concave down};\ y''>0\Rightarrow\text{concave up};\ \text{inflection where }y''\text{ changes sign}\)
Step 1: \(y'=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3)\Rightarrow\text{turning points }x=1,3\)
Step 2: \(y''=6x-12=0\Rightarrow x=2,\ y(2)=8-24+18+1=3\)
Step 3: \(x<2:\ y''<0\ (\text{concave down});\ x>2:\ y''>0\ (\text{concave up})\)
Worked derivation: \[y(1)=1-6+9+1=5,\quad y(3)=27-54+27+1=1\]
Check: \[\text{inflection is the midpoint of the turning points: }\left(\tfrac{1+3}{2},\tfrac{5+1}{2}\right)=(2,3)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a cubic is symmetric about its inflection point, which lies midway between its maximum and minimum}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(y''<0\text{ for }x<2\); (C) \((3,1)\text{ is the minimum}\); (D) \((1,5)\text{ is the maximum}\).
Key point: \(\text{inflection where }y''=0\text{ and changes sign; cubic: midpoint of turning points}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the intervals where a cubic is increasing or decreasing and its local extreme values from the sign of the derivative
questions.question: For \(f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+1\), on which intervals is \(f\) increasing, and what are its local maximum and minimum values?
options: A) increasing on \([2,3]\); maximum \(28\), minimum \(29\)
B) increasing on \((-\infty,2]\cup[3,\infty)\), decreasing on \([2,3]\); local maximum \(f(2)=29\), local minimum \(f(3)=28\)
C) increasing on \((-\infty,3]\); no local extremum
D) decreasing on \((-\infty,2]\cup[3,\infty)\); local maximum \(f(3)=28\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Increasing on \((-\infty,2]\cup[3,\infty)\); max \(29\) at \(x=2\), min \(28\) at \(x=3\).
Given: \(f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+1\)
Formula/Principle: \(f'(x)\ge0\Rightarrow\text{increasing};\ f'\text{ changes }+\to-\text{ at a maximum and }-\to+\text{ at a minimum}\)
Step 1: \(f'(x)=6x^2-30x+36=6(x-2)(x-3)\)
Step 2: \(f'>0\text{ for }x<2\text{ or }x>3;\ f'<0\text{ for }2<x<3\)
Step 3: \(f(2)=16-60+72+1=29,\ f(3)=54-135+108+1=28\)
Worked derivation: \[f''(x)=12x-30:\ f''(2)=-6<0\ (\max),\ f''(3)=6>0\ (\min)\]
Check: \[f(2)>f(3)\text{ as required for a max followed by a min}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the sign of }f'\text{ between its roots decides rising and falling stretches}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f\text{ decreases on }[2,3]\text{; values swapped}\); (C) \(f'\text{ changes sign at }2\text{ and }3\); (D) \(\text{intervals reversed}\).
Key point: \(f'=6(x-2)(x-3):\ \uparrow\text{ outside }[2,3],\ \downarrow\text{ inside}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Evaluating a symmetric definite integral with the property ∫₀^a f(x) dx = ∫₀^a f(a − x) dx and solving for the upper limit
questions.question: If \(\displaystyle\int_0^a\frac{\sqrt x}{\sqrt x+\sqrt{a-x}}\,dx=3\), what is the value of \(a\)?
options: C) \(\tfrac32\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(a=6\).
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^a\frac{\sqrt x}{\sqrt x+\sqrt{a-x}}\,dx=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\int_0^a f(x)\,dx=\int_0^a f(a-x)\,dx\)
Step 1: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^a\frac{\sqrt{a-x}}{\sqrt{a-x}+\sqrt x}\,dx\)
Step 2: \(2I=\displaystyle\int_0^a1\,dx=a\Rightarrow I=\dfrac a2\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac a2=3\Rightarrow a=6\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{\sqrt x}{\sqrt x+\sqrt{a-x}}+\frac{\sqrt{a-x}}{\sqrt{a-x}+\sqrt x}=1\]
Check: \[\text{integrand at }x=\tfrac a2\text{ is }\tfrac12;\ \text{average value }\tfrac12\Rightarrow I=\tfrac a2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{replacing }x\text{ by }a-x\text{ swaps numerator and the other term, so the two forms add to }1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{takes }I=a\); (B) \(\text{squares the answer}\); (C) \(\text{takes }I=2a\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int_0^a\frac{f(x)}{f(x)+f(a-x)}dx=\frac a2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the area enclosed between a parabola and a line through the origin as a function of the slope, and solving for the slope
questions.question: The area enclosed between \(y=x^2\) and \(y=kx\ (k>0)\) is \(36\) square units. What is \(k\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(k=6\).
Given: \(y=x^2,\ y=kx,\ k>0,\ \text{area}=36\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{area}=\displaystyle\int_a^b(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx\)
Step 1: \(x^2=kx\Rightarrow x=0,\ k;\ \text{line above parabola on }(0,k)\)
Step 2: \(\text{area}=\displaystyle\int_0^k(kx-x^2)\,dx=\frac{k^3}{2}-\frac{k^3}{3}=\frac{k^3}{6}\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac{k^3}{6}=36\Rightarrow k^3=216\Rightarrow k=6\)
Worked derivation: \[\int_0^6(6x-x^2)\,dx=\left[3x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^6=108-72=36\]
Check: \[x=3:\ 6x=18>x^2=9\Rightarrow\text{line is above the parabola}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the region lies between the two intersection points with the line on top}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gives area }4.5\); (B) \(\text{equates }k\text{ to the area}\); (C) \(\text{omits the factor }\tfrac16\).
Key point: \(\text{area between }y=x^2\text{ and }y=kx=\dfrac{k^3}{6}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Forming and solving a variable-separable differential equation for a curve from a geometric condition on its slope
questions.question: A curve passes through \((1,2)\) and its slope at every point \((x,y)\) with \(x>0\) is \(\dfrac{2y}{x}\). What is its equation and the value of \(y\) at \(x=2\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(y=2x^2\); \(y(2)=8\).
Given: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{2y}{x},\ y(1)=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{separate variables: }\displaystyle\int\frac{dy}{y}=\int\frac{2}{x}\,dx\)
Step 1: \(\ln|y|=2\ln|x|+c\)
Step 2: \(y=Cx^2\)
Step 3: \(2=C\cdot1\Rightarrow C=2\Rightarrow y=2x^2,\ y(2)=8\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dy}{dx}=4x=\frac{2\cdot2x^2}{x}=\frac{2y}{x}\]
Check: \[y(1)=2\cdot1=2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the slope condition separates into }\tfrac{dy}{y}=\tfrac{2\,dx}{x}\text{, giving a power law}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{slope would be }y/x\); (C) \(\text{slope }2x\ne\tfrac{2y}{x}\); (D) \(\text{slope would be }y\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{ny}{x}\Rightarrow y=Cx^n\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting subsets of a finite set under membership conditions, and intersecting two real intervals
questions.question: For \(A=\{1,2,3,4\}\), how many subsets does \(A\) have, how many contain \(1\) but not \(2\), and what is \([2,5)\cap(3,7]\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(16\); \(4\); \((3,5)\).
Given: \(A=\{1,2,3,4\},\ n(A)=4\)
Formula/Principle: \(n(P(A))=2^{n};\ \text{fixing membership of }k\text{ elements leaves }2^{n-k}\text{ subsets}\)
Step 1: \(n(P(A))=2^4=16\)
Step 2: \(1\in S,\ 2\notin S\text{ fixed; }3,4\text{ free}\Rightarrow2^2=4\)
Step 3: \([2,5)\cap(3,7]=\{x:3<x<5\}=(3,5)\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{subsets: }\{1\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{1,3,4\}\]
Check: \[3\notin(3,7],\ 5\notin[2,5)\Rightarrow\text{both ends open}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each free element is either in or out, doubling the count; an intersection keeps the stricter end at each side}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{forgets to fix }2\text{; ends wrongly closed}\); (C) \(\text{omits the empty set; }5\text{ excluded}\); (D) \(\text{uses }2^3\text{ and gives the union}\).
Key point: \(n(P(A))=2^n;\ \text{intersection: larger left end, smaller right end}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Values of the greatest integer function at negative arguments, the identity for [x] + [−x], and solving a quadratic in [x]
questions.question: For the greatest integer function \([x]\), what are \([x]+[-x]\) and \([-2.7]\), and what is the solution set of \([x]^2-5[x]+6=0\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(0\) or \(-1\); \([-2.7]=-3\); \(x\in[2,4)\).
Given: \([x]=\text{greatest integer}\le x\)
Formula/Principle: \([x]=n\iff n\le x<n+1\)
Step 1: \(x=n+f,\ 0<f<1:\ [x]=n,\ [-x]=-n-1\Rightarrow\text{sum }-1;\ f=0:\text{ sum }0\)
Step 2: \(-3\le-2.7<-2\Rightarrow[-2.7]=-3\)
Step 3: \(([x]-2)([x]-3)=0\Rightarrow[x]=2\text{ or }3\Rightarrow x\in[2,3)\cup[3,4)=[2,4)\)
Worked derivation: \[x=3.5:\ [x]=3,\ [-3.5]=-4,\ \text{sum}=-1\]
Check: \[x=3.99:\ [x]=3\Rightarrow9-15+6=0\ \checkmark;\ x=4:\ 16-20+6=2\ne0\]
Why: \(\text{the floor of a negative non-integer moves away from zero, and each integer value of }[x]\text{ covers a half-open interval}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{fails for non-integers; }[x]\text{ takes values on intervals}\); (B) \(\text{fails for integers; misses }[3,4)\); (D) \(\text{wrong sign and wrong endpoints}\).
Key point: \([x]+[-x]\in\{0,-1\};\ [x]=n\iff x\in[n,n+1)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the identity (1 + tan A)(1 + tan B) = 2 when A + B = 45° to evaluate a long product, and finding tan 75°
questions.question: What is the value of \(\displaystyle\prod_{k=1}^{44}(1+\tan k^\circ)\), and what is \(\tan75^\circ\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(2^{22}\); \(\tan75^\circ=2+\sqrt3\).
Given: \(k=1,\dots,44;\ A+B=45^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(\tan(A+B)=\dfrac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\tan B}\)
Step 1: \(\tan(A+B)=1\Rightarrow\tan A+\tan B+\tan A\tan B=1\)
Step 2: \((1+\tan A)(1+\tan B)=1+(\tan A+\tan B+\tan A\tan B)=2\)
Step 3: \(\text{pairs }(k,45-k),\ k=1..22\Rightarrow22\text{ pairs}\Rightarrow2^{22}\)
Worked derivation: \[\tan75^\circ=\frac{\tan45^\circ+\tan30^\circ}{1-\tan45^\circ\tan30^\circ}=\frac{1+\frac1{\sqrt3}}{1-\frac1{\sqrt3}}=\frac{\sqrt3+1}{\sqrt3-1}=2+\sqrt3\]
Check: \[(1+\tan22^\circ)(1+\tan23^\circ)\approx1.404\times1.424\approx2.00\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the 44 factors split exactly into 22 complementary-to-}45^\circ\text{ pairs, each giving }2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts each factor as 2; }2-\sqrt3=\tan15^\circ\); (B) \(\text{miscounts pairs}\); (D) \(\text{adds instead of multiplying}\).
Key point: \(A+B=45^\circ\Rightarrow(1+\tan A)(1+\tan B)=2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the real parameter for which a complex quotient is purely imaginary, and the modulus and principal argument of a complex number in the third quadrant
questions.question: For real \(k\), let \(z=\dfrac{k+2i}{1-i}\). For which \(k\) is \(z\) purely imaginary, can \(\arg z=\tfrac\pi4\) for some real \(k\), and what are the modulus and principal argument of \(-1-i\sqrt3\)?
options: A) \(k=2\) (then \(z=2i\)); \(\arg z=\tfrac\pi4\) is impossible; \(|-1-i\sqrt3|=2,\ \arg=-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
B) \(k=-2\); \(\arg z=\tfrac\pi4\) when \(k=0\); modulus \(2\), \(\arg=\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\)
C) \(k=2\); \(\arg z=\tfrac\pi4\) when \(k=2\); modulus \(4\), \(\arg=-\tfrac\pi3\)
D) no such \(k\); modulus \(\sqrt2\), \(\arg=\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k=2\); impossible; \(2,\ -\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\).
Given: \(z=\dfrac{k+2i}{1-i},\ w=-1-i\sqrt3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{multiply by the conjugate }1+i;\ \arg\in(-\pi,\pi]\)
Step 1: \(z=\dfrac{(k+2i)(1+i)}{2}=\dfrac{(k-2)+(k+2)i}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\operatorname{Re}z=0\Rightarrow k=2,\ z=\dfrac{4i}{2}=2i\)
Step 3: \(\arg z=\tfrac\pi4\Rightarrow k-2=k+2>0\Rightarrow-2=2\text{, impossible}\)
Worked derivation: \[|w|=\sqrt{1+3}=2;\ w\text{ in quadrant III},\ \alpha=\tan^{-1}\sqrt3=\tfrac\pi3\Rightarrow\arg w=-\left(\pi-\tfrac\pi3\right)=-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\]
Check: \[2\left(\cos\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)+i\sin\left(-\tfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right)=-1-i\sqrt3\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{real and imaginary parts of }z\text{ always differ by }2\text{, so they can never be equal}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(k=-2\text{ gives }z=-2\text{ (real); }\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\text{ is not principal}\); (C) \(k=2\text{ gives }\arg=\tfrac\pi2;\ |w|=2\); (D) \(k=2\text{ works}\).
Key point: \(\text{rationalise; principal arg in }(-\pi,\pi]\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting |z − a| = r as a circle and finding the common points of two circles in the Argand plane
questions.question: How many complex numbers satisfy both \(|z|=2\) and \(|z-2|=2\), and what are they?
options: A) none
B) exactly one, \(z=1\)
C) infinitely many, lying on the line \(\operatorname{Re}z=1\)
D) two: \(z=1\pm i\sqrt3\), which with \(0\) and \(2\) form two equilateral triangles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(z=1\pm i\sqrt3\).
Given: \(|z|=2,\ |z-2|=2\)
Formula/Principle: \(|z-a|=r\text{ is a circle with centre }a\text{ and radius }r\)
Step 1: \(\text{circles: centre }0,\ r=2;\ \text{centre }2,\ r=2;\ \text{distance between centres }2<4\Rightarrow\text{two common points}\)
Step 2: \(x^2+y^2=4,\ (x-2)^2+y^2=4\Rightarrow-4x+4=0\Rightarrow x=1\)
Step 3: \(y^2=3\Rightarrow y=\pm\sqrt3\)
Worked derivation: \[|1+i\sqrt3|=\sqrt{1+3}=2,\quad|1+i\sqrt3-2|=|-1+i\sqrt3|=2\]
Check: \[\text{sides }|z|=|z-2|=|2-0|=2\Rightarrow\text{equilateral}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{two equal circles whose centres are closer than the sum of radii cut in two points symmetric about the line of centres}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{circles do intersect}\); (B) \(|1|=1\ne2\); (C) \(\text{the line is only the common chord}\).
Key point: \(|z-a|=r\text{ is a circle; two circles meet in at most two points}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting committees with an "at least" condition by cases and by complement, and finding the largest binomial coefficient
questions.question: A committee of \(5\) is chosen from \(6\) men and \(4\) women so that it has at least \(2\) women. In how many ways can this be done, and for which \(r\) is \({}^{11}C_r\) largest?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(186\); \({}^{11}C_5={}^{11}C_6=462\).
Given: \(6\text{ men},\ 4\text{ women},\ \text{committee }5,\ \ge2\text{ women}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{sum over cases, or total minus unwanted cases};\ {}^{n}C_r\text{ largest at }r=\tfrac{n\pm1}{2}\text{ for odd }n\)
Step 1: \(2W:\ {}^4C_2\,{}^6C_3=6\cdot20=120;\ 3W:\ {}^4C_3\,{}^6C_2=4\cdot15=60;\ 4W:\ {}^4C_4\,{}^6C_1=6\)
Step 2: \(120+60+6=186\)
Step 3: \(n=11\text{ odd}\Rightarrow r=5,6;\ {}^{11}C_5=\dfrac{11\cdot10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7}{120}=462\)
Worked derivation: \[{}^{10}C_5-\left({}^6C_5+{}^4C_1\,{}^6C_4\right)=252-(6+60)=186\]
Check: \[\text{direct cases and complement agree: }186\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{"at least" conditions are counted by splitting into exact cases or subtracting the excluded ones}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{counts only exactly 2 women}\); (C) \(\text{adds the excluded cases}\); (D) \(\text{gives the excluded count}\).
Key point: \(\text{at least }k=\text{total}-\text{fewer than }k;\ {}^{n}C_r\text{ max at middle}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Using the general term of a binomial expansion to find the constant term, count terms with positive powers, and write the middle terms
questions.question: In the expansion of \(\left(x^2+\dfrac1x\right)^9\), what is the constant term, how many terms have a positive power of \(x\), and what are the middle terms?
options: A) constant term \(126\); \(5\) positive-power terms; middle term \(84x^3\)
B) constant term \(84\); \(6\) positive-power terms; middle terms \(126x^6\) and \(126x^3\)
C) constant term \(36\); \(4\) positive-power terms; middle term \(126x^0\)
D) no constant term; \(9\) positive-power terms; middle terms \(84x^6\) and \(84x^3\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(84\); \(6\) terms; \(126x^6,\ 126x^3\).
Given: \(\left(x^2+x^{-1}\right)^9,\ n=9\)
Formula/Principle: \(T_{r+1}={}^9C_r\,(x^2)^{9-r}(x^{-1})^r={}^9C_r\,x^{18-3r}\)
Step 1: \(18-3r=0\Rightarrow r=6\Rightarrow{}^9C_6=84\)
Step 2: \(18-3r>0\Rightarrow r<6\Rightarrow r=0,1,\dots,5\Rightarrow6\text{ terms}\)
Step 3: \(n=9\text{ odd}\Rightarrow\text{middle terms }T_5,T_6:\ {}^9C_4x^6=126x^6,\ {}^9C_5x^3=126x^3\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{powers: }18,15,12,9,6,3,0,-3,-6,-9\ \ (r=0\dots9)\]
Check: \[10\text{ terms}=6\text{ positive}+1\text{ constant}+3\text{ negative}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the exponent of }x\text{ falls by 3 with each term, so the general term locates every required term}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{coefficients swapped; miscounts}\); (C) \(\text{wrong }r\); (D) \(r=6\text{ gives a constant term}\).
Key point: \(T_{r+1}={}^nC_r\,a^{n-r}b^r;\ \text{odd }n\text{ has two middle terms}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the eccentricity, foci, latus rectum and lattice points of an ellipse in standard form
questions.question: For the ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=1\), what are its eccentricity, the number of points with integer coordinates on it, and the length of its latus rectum?
options: A) \(e=\tfrac34\); \(8\) lattice points; latus rectum \(\tfrac92\)
B) \(e=\tfrac54\); \(4\) lattice points; latus rectum \(\tfrac{32}{3}\)
C) \(e=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{4}\) (foci \((\pm\sqrt7,0)\)); \(4\) lattice points; latus rectum \(\tfrac92\)
D) \(e=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{3}\); \(4\) lattice points; latus rectum \(\tfrac{9}{4}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(e=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{4}\); \(4\); \(\tfrac92\).
Given: \(a^2=16,\ b^2=9,\ a=4,\ b=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(c^2=a^2-b^2,\ e=\tfrac ca,\ \text{latus rectum}=\dfrac{2b^2}{a}\)
Step 1: \(c=\sqrt{16-9}=\sqrt7\Rightarrow e=\tfrac{\sqrt7}{4}\)
Step 2: \(\text{latus rectum}=\dfrac{2\cdot9}{4}=\dfrac92\)
Step 3: \(x\in\{0,\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,\pm4\}:\ y^2=9\left(1-\tfrac{x^2}{16}\right)=9,\tfrac{135}{16},\tfrac{27}{4},\tfrac{63}{16},0\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{integer }y\text{ only for }x=0\ (y=\pm3)\text{ and }x=\pm4\ (y=0)\Rightarrow(0,\pm3),(\pm4,0)\]
Check: \[e<1\ \checkmark;\ \text{latus rectum }\tfrac92<2b=6\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{only the vertices make }9(1-x^2/16)\text{ a perfect square}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(e=\tfrac ba\text{ is wrong; extra lattice points}\); (B) \(e>1\text{ is a hyperbola}\); (D) \(\text{divides by }b\text{ instead of }a\).
Key point: \(e=\sqrt{1-b^2/a^2};\ \text{LR}=2b^2/a\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting points where a sum of modulus functions fails to be differentiable by examining each corner
questions.question: At how many real points is \(f(x)=|x^2-4|+|x|\) not differentiable?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(3\) points, \(x=-2,0,2\).
Given: \(f(x)=|x^2-4|+|x|\)
Formula/Principle: \(|g(x)|\text{ has a corner where }g\text{ has a simple zero; a sum is non-differentiable where exactly one term has a corner}\)
Step 1: \(x^2-4=0\Rightarrow x=\pm2\text{ (simple zeros); }|x|\text{ smooth there}\)
Step 2: \(|x|\text{ has a corner at }0;\ |x^2-4|=4-x^2\text{ smooth near }0\)
Step 3: \(\text{corners do not coincide}\Rightarrow\text{no cancellation}\Rightarrow3\text{ points}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{at }x=2:\ f'(2^-)=-2x+1=-3,\ f'(2^+)=2x+1=5;\quad\text{at }x=0:\ f'(0^-)=-1,\ f'(0^+)=1\]
Check: \[x=-2:\ f'(-2^-)=2x-1=-5,\ f'(-2^+)=-2x-1=3\ \Rightarrow\text{corner}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each corner of one term survives because the other term is smooth there}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{misses the corner of }|x|\); (C) \(\text{misses }\pm2\); (D) \(x=\pm1\text{ are smooth points}\).
Key point: \(\text{non-differentiable at simple zeros inside moduli unless corners cancel}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Computing mean, median, range, and mean deviation about the mean and about the median for ungrouped data
questions.question: For the data \(3,5,6,8,11,12,18\), what are the mean, the mean deviation about the mean, the median, the mean deviation about the median and the range?
options: D) mean \(9\), MD about mean \(4\), median \(8\), MD about median \(\tfrac{27}{7}\approx3.86\), range \(15\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(9,\ 4,\ 8,\ \tfrac{27}{7},\ 15\).
Given: \(3,5,6,8,11,12,18;\ n=7\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{MD}(a)=\dfrac1n\sum|x_i-a|\)
Step 1: \(\bar x=\dfrac{63}{7}=9;\ \text{median}=4\text{th value}=8;\ \text{range}=18-3=15\)
Step 2: \(\sum|x_i-9|=6+4+3+1+2+3+9=28\Rightarrow\text{MD}=4\)
Step 3: \(\sum|x_i-8|=5+3+2+0+3+4+10=27\Rightarrow\text{MD}=\tfrac{27}{7}\)
Worked derivation: \[\tfrac{27}{7}\approx3.86<4\]
Check: \[\text{MD about the median is the least of all mean deviations}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the sum of absolute deviations is minimised at the median}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{mean and median swapped}\); (B) \(\text{MDs swapped; wrong range}\); (C) \(\text{wrong sums}\).
Key point: \(\text{MD about median}\le\text{MD about mean}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding probabilities of the union, of neither event, and of exactly one event from P(A), P(B) and P(A∩B), and testing independence
questions.question: If \(P(A)=0.5,\ P(B)=0.4\) and \(P(A\cap B)=0.2\), what are \(P(A\cup B)\), \(P(\text{neither})\) and \(P(\text{exactly one})\), and are \(A,B\) independent?
options: A) \(0.9,\ 0.1,\ 0.7\); not independent
C) \(0.7,\ 0.2,\ 0.5\); not independent
D) \(0.7,\ 0.3,\ 0.5\); independent, since \(P(A)P(B)=0.2=P(A\cap B)\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(0.7,\ 0.3,\ 0.5\); independent.
Given: \(P(A)=0.5,\ P(B)=0.4,\ P(A\cap B)=0.2\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B);\ P(\text{exactly one})=P(A\cup B)-P(A\cap B)\)
Step 1: \(P(A\cup B)=0.5+0.4-0.2=0.7\)
Step 2: \(P(\text{neither})=1-0.7=0.3\)
Step 3: \(P(\text{exactly one})=0.7-0.2=0.5\)
Worked derivation: \[P(A)P(B)=0.5\times0.4=0.2=P(A\cap B)\Rightarrow\text{independent};\ P(A\mid B)=\tfrac{0.2}{0.4}=0.5=P(A)\]
Check: \[0.3+0.5+0.2=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{neither, exactly one and both are mutually exclusive and exhaustive}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{ignores the overlap}\); (B) \(\text{exactly one wrong}\); (C) \(\text{neither wrong; they are independent}\).
Key point: \(\text{exactly one}=P(A)+P(B)-2P(A\cap B)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Computing the probability that two numbers chosen without replacement have an even sum, and its limiting value as the range grows
questions.question: Two different numbers are chosen at random from \(1,2,\dots,20\). What is the probability that their sum is even, and what does this probability approach for numbers chosen from \(1,\dots,2n\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
options: A) \(\tfrac12\); stays \(\tfrac12\)
B) \(\tfrac{9}{19}\); tends to \(\tfrac12\)
D) \(\tfrac{9}{38}\); tends to \(\tfrac14\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\tfrac{9}{19}\); \(\to\tfrac12\).
Given: \(10\text{ odd and }10\text{ even numbers};\ 2\text{ chosen}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{sum even}\iff\text{both odd or both even}\)
Step 1: \(\text{favourable}=2\cdot{}^{10}C_2=90\)
Step 2: \(\text{total}={}^{20}C_2=190\Rightarrow P=\dfrac{90}{190}=\dfrac{9}{19}\)
Step 3: \(\text{for }1..2n:\ P=\dfrac{2\,{}^nC_2}{{}^{2n}C_2}=\dfrac{n(n-1)}{n(2n-1)}=\dfrac{n-1}{2n-1}\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n-1}{2n-1}=\frac12\]
Check: \[n=10:\ \frac{9}{19}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{choosing without replacement makes a same-parity second pick slightly less likely than }\tfrac12\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{assumes replacement}\); (C) \(\text{that is the odd-sum probability}\); (D) \(\text{counts only one parity}\).
Key point: \(P(\text{even sum})=\dfrac{n-1}{2n-1}<\dfrac12\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the parameter values for which a 3×3 linear system has a unique solution, infinitely many solutions or no solution
questions.question: For the system \(x+y+z=5,\ x+2y+4z=11,\ x+3y+kz=\mu\), for which values of \(k\) and \(\mu\) does it have a unique solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solution?
options: A) unique if \(k\ne7\); infinitely many if \(k=7,\ \mu=17\); no solution if \(k=7,\ \mu\ne17\)
B) unique if \(k\ne5\); infinitely many if \(k=5,\ \mu=11\)
C) unique for all \(k\); no solution never occurs
D) unique if \(k\ne7\); infinitely many if \(k=7,\ \mu\ne17\); no solution if \(k=7,\ \mu=17\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k\ne7\) unique; \(k=7,\mu=17\) infinite; \(k=7,\mu\ne17\) none.
Given: \(\text{coefficient matrix rows }(1,1,1),(1,2,4),(1,3,k)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\det A\ne0\Rightarrow\text{unique};\ \det A=0\Rightarrow\text{check consistency}\)
Step 1: \(\det A=1(2k-12)-1(k-4)+1(3-2)=k-7\)
Step 2: \(k=7:\ R_2-R_1:\ y+3z=6;\ R_3-R_2:\ y+3z=\mu-11\)
Step 3: \(\text{consistent}\iff\mu-11=6\iff\mu=17\)
Worked derivation: \[k=7,\ \mu=17:\ z=t,\ y=6-3t,\ x=5-y-z=-1+2t\ \ (t\in\mathbb R)\]
Check: \[t=0:\ (-1,6,0):\ -1+6+0=5,\ -1+12+0=11,\ -1+18+0=17\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{when the determinant vanishes, the planes either share a line or have no common point depending on the constant}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\det=0\text{ at }k=7\); (C) \(\det\text{ vanishes at }k=7\); (D) \(\text{consistency conditions reversed}\).
Key point: \(\det=0\text{ and consistent}\Rightarrow\infty;\ \det=0\text{ and inconsistent}\Rightarrow\text{none}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Solving a 3×3 system with non-zero determinant and interpreting the solution as the single common point of three planes
questions.question: For the system \(x+y+z=6,\ x-y+z=2,\ 2x+y-z=1\), what is the determinant of the coefficient matrix, the solution, and its geometric meaning?
options: A) \(\det=0\); infinitely many solutions on a line
B) \(\det=-6\); solution \((2,1,3)\); planes meet in a line
C) \(\det=6\); unique solution \((1,2,3)\): the three planes pass through exactly one common point
D) \(\det=6\); solution \((3,2,1)\); the planes are parallel
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(\det=6\); \((1,2,3)\); one common point.
Given: \(\text{rows }(1,1,1),(1,-1,1),(2,1,-1);\ \text{constants }6,2,1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\det A\ne0\Rightarrow X=A^{-1}B\text{ unique}\)
Step 1: \(\det A=1(1-1)-1(-1-2)+1(1+2)=0+3+3=6\)
Step 2: \((1)-(2):\ 2y=4\Rightarrow y=2\)
Step 3: \(x+z=4,\ 2x-z=-1\Rightarrow3x=3\Rightarrow x=1,\ z=3\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{Cramer: }x=\frac{D_x}{D},\ D_x=\begin{vmatrix}6&1&1\\2&-1&1\\1&1&-1\end{vmatrix}=6(0)-1(-3)+1(3)=6\Rightarrow x=1\]
Check: \[1+2+3=6,\ 1-2+3=2,\ 2+2-3=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a non-zero determinant means the three normals are independent, so the planes meet in a single point}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\det\ne0\); (B) \(\text{sign and solution wrong}\); (D) \((3,2,1)\text{ fails the second equation; planes are not parallel}\).
Key point: \(\det\ne0\Rightarrow\text{unique solution}=\text{one common point of three planes}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Relating the potential energy curve of a spring to the restoring force through F = −dU/dx, and the shapes of U(x) and F(x) graphs
questions.question: A block on a spring of constant \(k\) is displaced \(x\) from equilibrium. How are the graphs of potential energy \(U\) and spring force \(F\) against \(x\) related, and what is the work done by the spring as it is stretched from \(0\) to \(x\)?
options: A) \(U=\tfrac12kx^2\) is a parabola with its minimum at \(x=0\); \(F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx}=-kx\) is a straight line of slope \(-k\), zero at equilibrium and always directed towards it; the work done by the spring from \(0\) to \(x\) is \(-\tfrac12kx^2\)
B) \(U=kx\) is a straight line; \(F=-\tfrac12kx^2\)
C) \(U\) is maximum at \(x=0\), so equilibrium is unstable
D) \(F=+\dfrac{dU}{dx}\), so the force points away from equilibrium; the work done by the spring is \(+\tfrac12kx^2\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(U\) parabola with minimum at \(0\); \(F=-kx\) line; \(W_{\text{spring}}=-\tfrac12kx^2\).
Given: \(\text{spring constant }k,\ \text{displacement }x\)
Formula/Principle: \(F=-kx;\ F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx};\ W=\displaystyle\int F\,dx\)
Step 1: \(W_{\text{spring}}=\displaystyle\int_0^x(-kx)\,dx=-\tfrac12kx^2\)
Step 2: \(U=-W_{\text{spring}}=\tfrac12kx^2\)
Step 3: \(-\dfrac{dU}{dx}=-kx=F\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dU}{dx}=0\text{ at }x=0,\ \frac{d^2U}{dx^2}=k>0\Rightarrow\text{minimum}\Rightarrow\text{stable equilibrium}\]
Check: \[x>0:\ F<0;\ x<0:\ F>0\Rightarrow\text{always restoring}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the force is minus the slope of the potential energy curve, so it always points downhill towards the minimum}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{forms of }U\text{ and }F\text{ interchanged}\); (C) \(U\text{ is minimum, so equilibrium is stable}\); (D) \(\text{sign error; the spring does negative work when stretched}\).
Key point: \(F=-\dfrac{dU}{dx};\ \text{stable equilibrium at a minimum of }U\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.sub_topic: Applying conservation of angular momentum to a contracting star and a spinning skater, and finding the change in rotational kinetic energy
questions.question: A star of radius \(R\) rotating once in \(25\) days collapses, with no external torque and uniform density, to radius \(\tfrac{R}{100}\). Separately, a skater pulls in her arms so that her moment of inertia halves. What is the new period of the star, and how do the skater's angular speed and kinetic energy change?
options: A) \(0.25\) day; skater's \(\omega\) and KE unchanged
B) \(2.5\times10^{-3}\) day; \(\omega\) doubles, KE unchanged
C) \(25\) days; \(\omega\) halves, KE halves
D) about \(216\ \text{s}\) (period reduced \(10^4\) times); skater's \(\omega\) doubles and her rotational KE doubles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(T'\approx216\ \text{s}\); \(\omega\) doubles; KE doubles.
Given: \(T=25\ \text{days}=2.16\times10^6\ \text{s},\ R'=\tfrac{R}{100};\ I'=\tfrac I2\)
Formula/Principle: \(L=I\omega=\text{constant};\ I\propto MR^2;\ K=\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\)
Step 1: \(\omega'=\omega\dfrac{I}{I'}=\omega\left(\dfrac{R}{R'}\right)^2=10^4\omega\)
Step 2: \(T'=\dfrac{T}{10^4}=\dfrac{2.16\times10^6}{10^4}=216\ \text{s}\)
Step 3: \(\text{skater: }\omega'=2\omega;\ K'=\dfrac{L^2}{2(I/2)}=2K\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{K'}{K}=\frac{\tfrac12I'\omega'^2}{\tfrac12I\omega^2}=\frac{\tfrac12\cdot4}{1}=2\]
Check: \[L'=\tfrac I2\cdot2\omega=I\omega=L\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{with no external torque }L\text{ is conserved; the extra kinetic energy comes from internal work done in pulling mass inward}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }R/R'\text{ instead of its square}\); (B) \(\text{KE changes when }I\text{ changes at constant }L\); (C) \(\text{ignores conservation of }L\).
Key point: \(I\omega=\text{constant};\ K=\dfrac{L^2}{2I}\uparrow\text{ as }I\downarrow\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the decrease of g with height and with depth for small distances, and the values at height R and at the centre of the Earth
questions.question: Taking \(R=6400\ \text{km}\), at what height and at what depth is \(g\) reduced by \(1\%\), and what is \(g\) at height \(R\) and at the centre?
options: A) height \(64\ \text{km}\), depth \(32\ \text{km}\); \(\tfrac g2\) at height \(R\); \(g\) at the centre
B) height \(32\ \text{km}\), depth \(32\ \text{km}\); \(\tfrac g4\) at height \(R\); \(\tfrac g2\) at the centre
C) height \(32\ \text{km}\), depth \(64\ \text{km}\); \(\tfrac g4\) at height \(R\); zero at the centre
D) height \(64\ \text{km}\), depth \(64\ \text{km}\); \(\tfrac g2\) at height \(R\); zero at the centre
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(h=32\ \text{km},\ d=64\ \text{km}\); \(\tfrac g4\); \(0\).
Given: \(R=6400\ \text{km},\ \dfrac{\Delta g}{g}=0.01\)
Formula/Principle: \(g_h\approx g\left(1-\dfrac{2h}{R}\right)\ (h\ll R);\ g_d=g\left(1-\dfrac dR\right);\ g_h=\dfrac{g}{(1+h/R)^2}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2h}{R}=0.01\Rightarrow h=0.005\times6400=32\ \text{km}\)
Step 2: \(\dfrac dR=0.01\Rightarrow d=64\ \text{km}\)
Step 3: \(h=R:\ g_h=\dfrac{g}{4};\ d=R:\ g_d=0\)
Worked derivation: \[g_d=\frac{GM}{R^3}(R-d)\Rightarrow g\propto r\text{ inside};\quad g_h=\frac{GM}{(R+h)^2}\Rightarrow g\propto\frac1{r^2}\text{ outside}\]
Check: \[\text{for the same small distance, }g\text{ falls twice as fast with height as with depth}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{going up increases distance from the whole mass, while going down removes the outer shell, whose net pull is zero}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{height and depth swapped; }g\text{ is zero at the centre}\); (B) \(\text{equal values wrong}\); (D) \(\text{wrong height and value at }R\).
Key point: \(\text{small }h:\ \Delta g/g=2h/R;\ \text{depth}:\ \Delta g/g=d/R\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding efflux speed by Torricelli's law and the horizontal range of jets from holes at different depths in a tall tank
questions.question: A tank stands on the ground and is filled with water to height \(H=10\ \text{m}\). (\(g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)) What is the efflux speed from a hole \(5\ \text{m}\) below the surface, and how do the ranges of jets from holes \(2\ \text{m}\) and \(8\ \text{m}\) below the surface compare?
options: A) \(\sqrt{50}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); the deeper hole has the larger range
B) \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); both jets land \(8\ \text{m}\) from the tank, since range \(=2\sqrt{h(H-h)}\) is the same for depths \(h\) and \(H-h\)
C) \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); the shallower hole has twice the range
D) \(100\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); both land \(10\ \text{m}\) away
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); both ranges \(8\ \text{m}\).
Given: \(H=10\ \text{m},\ h=5\ \text{m};\ h_1=2\ \text{m},\ h_2=8\ \text{m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(v=\sqrt{2gh};\ \text{fall height }H-h,\ t=\sqrt{\dfrac{2(H-h)}{g}};\ R=vt=2\sqrt{h(H-h)}\)
Step 1: \(v=\sqrt{2\cdot10\cdot5}=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(R_1=2\sqrt{2\cdot8}=8\ \text{m}\)
Step 3: \(R_2=2\sqrt{8\cdot2}=8\ \text{m}\)
Worked derivation: \[R=\sqrt{2gh}\sqrt{\frac{2(H-h)}{g}}=2\sqrt{h(H-h)};\ \frac{dR}{dh}=0\Rightarrow h=\frac H2\Rightarrow R_{\max}=H=10\ \text{m}\]
Check: \[h=2:\ v=\sqrt{40},\ t=\sqrt{1.6},\ R=\sqrt{64}=8\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a deeper hole gives a faster jet but less fall time; the product is symmetric about mid-height}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }v=\sqrt{gh}\); (C) \(\text{ranges are equal}\); (D) \(\text{omits the square root; }10\ \text{m is only the maximum range}\).
Key point: \(v=\sqrt{2gh};\ R=2\sqrt{h(H-h)}\text{ symmetric about }H/2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the principle of calorimetry with a change of state to find the final temperature when ice is added to warm water
questions.question: \(30\ \text{g}\) of ice at \(0^\circ\text{C}\) is added to \(150\ \text{g}\) of water at \(40^\circ\text{C}\) in a vessel of negligible heat capacity. (\(L_f=336\ \text{J g}^{-1},\ c=4.2\ \text{J g}^{-1}\,{}^\circ\text{C}^{-1}\)) What is the final temperature?
options: A) \(0^\circ\text{C}\), with some ice left
B) \(33.3^\circ\text{C}\)
C) \(20^\circ\text{C}\)
D) \(26.7^\circ\text{C}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(20^\circ\text{C}\).
Given: \(m_i=30\ \text{g},\ m_w=150\ \text{g},\ T_w=40^\circ\text{C},\ L_f=336,\ c=4.2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{heat lost}=\text{heat gained};\ Q=mL,\ Q=mc\Delta T\)
Step 1: \(\text{heat available cooling water to }0^\circ\text{C}=150\cdot4.2\cdot40=25\,200\ \text{J}\)
Step 2: \(\text{heat to melt ice}=30\cdot336=10\,080\ \text{J}<25\,200\Rightarrow\text{all ice melts}\)
