Step 3: \(150\cdot4.2(40-T)=10\,080+30\cdot4.2\cdot T\Rightarrow25\,200-630T=10\,080+126T\)
Worked derivation: \[756\,T=15\,120\Rightarrow T=20^\circ\text{C}\]
Check: \[\text{lost}=150\cdot4.2\cdot20=12\,600;\ \text{gained}=10\,080+30\cdot4.2\cdot20=12\,600\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the latent heat absorbed by melting comes first; the remaining heat warms the combined }180\ \text{g of water}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{enough heat is available to melt all the ice}\); (B) \(\text{ignores latent heat}\); (D) \(\text{omits warming the melted ice}\).
Key point: \(\text{check whether all ice melts before equating heats}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Applying the first law of thermodynamics to an isobaric process of an ideal monatomic gas
questions.question: \(2\) mol of an ideal monatomic gas is heated at constant pressure from \(300\ \text{K}\) to \(400\ \text{K}\). (\(R=8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)) What are the heat supplied, the work done by the gas and the change in internal energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(Q=4157\ \text{J},\ W=1663\ \text{J},\ \Delta U=2494\ \text{J}\).
Given: \(n=2,\ \Delta T=100\ \text{K},\ C_v=\tfrac32R,\ C_p=\tfrac52R\)
Formula/Principle: \(Q=nC_p\Delta T;\ W=P\Delta V=nR\Delta T;\ \Delta U=nC_v\Delta T;\ Q=\Delta U+W\)
Step 1: \(Q=2\cdot\tfrac52\cdot8.314\cdot100=4157\ \text{J}\)
Step 2: \(W=2\cdot8.314\cdot100=1663\ \text{J}\)
Step 3: \(\Delta U=2\cdot\tfrac32\cdot8.314\cdot100=2494\ \text{J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U+W=2494+1663=4157=Q\]
Check: \[\frac{W}{Q}=\frac{R}{C_p}=\frac25=0.4;\ \frac{1663}{4157}=0.40\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{at constant pressure, part of the heat raises internal energy and the rest does expansion work}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{describes a constant-volume process}\); (C) \(W\text{ and }\Delta U\text{ swapped}\); (D) \(\Delta U\text{ taken as }nC_p\Delta T\text{, which double counts the work}\).
Key point: \(\text{isobaric: }Q:\Delta U:W=C_p:C_v:R=5:3:2\text{ (monatomic)}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the shapes of acceleration–displacement, velocity–displacement and energy–displacement graphs in simple harmonic motion
questions.question: For a particle in SHM \(x=A\sin\omega t\), what are the shapes of the graphs of acceleration against displacement, velocity against displacement and kinetic energy against displacement?
options: A) \(a\) vs \(x\): parabola; \(v\) vs \(x\): straight line; KE vs \(x\): circle
B) \(a\) vs \(x\): straight line through the origin with positive slope \(\omega^2\); \(v\) vs \(x\): hyperbola
C) all three are sinusoidal curves

D) \(a\) vs \(x\): straight line through the origin with slope \(-\omega^2\); \(v\) vs \(x\): ellipse \(\dfrac{x^2}{A^2}+\dfrac{v^2}{\omega^2A^2}=1\) (a circle if \(\omega=1\) in suitable units); KE vs \(x\): downward parabola \(\tfrac12m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)\), zero at \(x=\pm A\) and maximum at \(x=0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Line of slope \(-\omega^2\); ellipse; downward parabola.
Given: \(x=A\sin\omega t\)
Formula/Principle: \(a=-\omega^2x;\ v=\pm\omega\sqrt{A^2-x^2};\ K=\tfrac12mv^2\)
Step 1: \(a=\ddot x=-\omega^2A\sin\omega t=-\omega^2x\Rightarrow\text{line, slope }-\omega^2\)
Step 2: \(v^2=\omega^2(A^2-x^2)\Rightarrow\dfrac{x^2}{A^2}+\dfrac{v^2}{\omega^2A^2}=1\Rightarrow\text{ellipse}\)
Step 3: \(K=\tfrac12m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)\Rightarrow\text{downward parabola}\)
Worked derivation: \[\cos^2\omega t+\sin^2\omega t=1\Rightarrow\left(\frac{v}{\omega A}\right)^2+\left(\frac xA\right)^2=1\]
Check: \[x=0:\ v=\pm\omega A,\ K_{\max}=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2;\ x=\pm A:\ v=0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{SHM is defined by acceleration proportional to and opposite to displacement; eliminating time gives the other shapes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{shapes mismatched}\); (B) \(\text{slope must be negative; }v\text{ vs }x\text{ is an ellipse}\); (C) \(\text{sinusoidal only against time}\).
Key point: \(a=-\omega^2x;\ v\text{–}x\text{ ellipse};\ K\text{–}x\text{ parabola}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding wavelength, speed of sound and end correction from the first two resonance lengths of a closed resonance tube
questions.question: A tuning fork of \(500\ \text{Hz}\) gives resonance in a closed resonance tube at air-column lengths \(16.0\ \text{cm}\) and \(50.0\ \text{cm}\). What are the wavelength, the speed of sound and the end correction?
options: B) \(\lambda=68\ \text{cm},\ v=340\ \text{m s}^{-1},\ e=1.0\ \text{cm}\)
C) \(\lambda=34\ \text{cm},\ v=170\ \text{m s}^{-1},\ e=1.0\ \text{cm}\)
D) \(\lambda=100\ \text{cm},\ v=500\ \text{m s}^{-1},\ e=2.0\ \text{cm}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(\lambda=68\ \text{cm},\ v=340\ \text{m s}^{-1},\ e=1\ \text{cm}\).
Given: \(f=500\ \text{Hz},\ l_1=16.0\ \text{cm},\ l_2=50.0\ \text{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(l_1+e=\dfrac\lambda4;\ l_2+e=\dfrac{3\lambda}4;\ v=f\lambda\)
Step 1: \(l_2-l_1=\dfrac\lambda2\Rightarrow\lambda=2(34.0)=68.0\ \text{cm}\)
Step 2: \(v=500\times0.68=340\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(e=\dfrac\lambda4-l_1=17.0-16.0=1.0\ \text{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[e=\frac{l_2-3l_1}{2}=\frac{50-48}{2}=1.0\ \text{cm}\]
Check: \[l_2+e=51=\tfrac34(68)\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the difference of successive resonance lengths removes the unknown end correction}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }4l_1\text{ ignoring end correction}\); (C) \(\text{takes }l_2-l_1=\lambda\); (D) \(\text{uses }2l_2\).
Key point: \(\lambda=2(l_2-l_1);\ e=\dfrac{l_2-3l_1}{2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding electric field from the force on a small test charge and then the source charge using Coulomb's law
questions.question: A test charge of \(2\ \text{nC}\) placed \(0.3\ \text{m}\) from a point charge \(Q\) experiences a force of \(6\times10^{-5}\ \text{N}\). What is the field at that point and the value of \(Q\)? (\(\tfrac1{4\pi\varepsilon_0}=9\times10^9\ \text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-2}\))
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(E=3\times10^4\ \text{N C}^{-1},\ Q=3\times10^{-7}\ \text{C}\).
Given: \(q=2\times10^{-9}\ \text{C},\ F=6\times10^{-5}\ \text{N},\ r=0.3\ \text{m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(E=\dfrac Fq;\ E=\dfrac{kQ}{r^2}\)
Step 1: \(E=\dfrac{6\times10^{-5}}{2\times10^{-9}}=3\times10^4\ \text{N C}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(Q=\dfrac{Er^2}{k}=\dfrac{3\times10^4\times0.09}{9\times10^9}\)
Step 3: \(Q=3\times10^{-7}\ \text{C}\)
Worked derivation: \[F=\frac{kQq}{r^2}=\frac{9\times10^9\cdot3\times10^{-7}\cdot2\times10^{-9}}{0.09}=6\times10^{-5}\ \text{N}\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{\text{N}}{\text{C}}\cdot\frac{\text{m}^2}{\text{N m}^2\text{C}^{-2}}=\text{C}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the field is force per unit test charge and depends only on the source charge and distance}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{multiplies instead of dividing}\); (C) \(\text{omits }r^2\text{ correctly}\); (D) \(\text{wrong power of ten}\).
Key point: \(E=F/q=kQ/r^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating the electrostatic potential energy of four equal charges at the corners of a square, and properties of equipotential surfaces
questions.question: Four charges of \(1\ \mu\text{C}\) each are placed at the corners of a square of side \(0.1\ \text{m}\). What is the electrostatic potential energy of the system, and which property of equipotential surfaces is correct? (\(k=9\times10^9\))
options: A) \(U=\dfrac{kq^2}{a}\left(4+\sqrt2\right)\approx0.487\ \text{J}\); equipotential surfaces are perpendicular to field lines, and no work is done in moving a charge along one
B) \(U=0.36\ \text{J}\); field lines are parallel to equipotential surfaces
C) \(U=0.54\ \text{J}\); work is needed to move a charge along an equipotential
D) \(U=0\), since the arrangement is symmetric; equipotentials can intersect
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(U\approx0.487\ \text{J}\); equipotentials \(\perp\) field, no work along them.
Given: \(q=10^{-6}\ \text{C},\ a=0.1\ \text{m};\ 4\text{ sides}+2\text{ diagonals}\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\sum_{\text{pairs}}\dfrac{kq_iq_j}{r_{ij}}\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{kq^2}{a}=\dfrac{9\times10^9\times10^{-12}}{0.1}=0.09\ \text{J}\)
Step 2: \(\text{sides: }4\times0.09;\ \text{diagonals }(a\sqrt2):\ 2\times\dfrac{0.09}{\sqrt2}=0.09\sqrt2\)
Step 3: \(U=0.09(4+\sqrt2)=0.09\times5.414=0.487\ \text{J}\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{pairs}={}^4C_2=6=4\text{ sides}+2\text{ diagonals}\]
Check: \[\text{all charges alike}\Rightarrow U>0\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the work to assemble the charges equals the sum over every pair; field lines cross equipotentials at right angles because }W=q\Delta V=0\text{ along them}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{counts only sides}\); (C) \(\text{wrong count; no work along equipotentials}\); (D) \(\text{like charges give positive energy; equipotentials never intersect}\).
Key point: \(\text{square: }U=\dfrac{kq^2}{a}(4+\sqrt2)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Finding the magnetic moment of a current-carrying coil, the torque in a uniform field as a function of angle, and the work to turn it from stable to unstable equilibrium
questions.question: A coil of \(50\) turns, area \(0.01\ \text{m}^2\), carrying \(0.2\ \text{A}\), is placed in a uniform field \(B=0.2\ \text{T}\). What are its magnetic moment, the maximum torque, and the work needed to turn it from \(\theta=0\) to \(\theta=180^\circ\)?
options: C) \(m=NIA=0.1\ \text{A m}^2;\ \tau_{\max}=mB=0.02\ \text{N m}\) (at \(\theta=90^\circ\), since \(\tau=mB\sin\theta\)); \(U=-mB\cos\theta\), so \(W=2mB=0.04\ \text{J}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(m=0.1\ \text{A m}^2,\ \tau_{\max}=0.02\ \text{N m},\ W=0.04\ \text{J}\).
Given: \(N=50,\ A=0.01\ \text{m}^2,\ I=0.2\ \text{A},\ B=0.2\ \text{T}\)
Formula/Principle: \(m=NIA;\ \tau=mB\sin\theta;\ U=-mB\cos\theta\)
Step 1: \(m=50\times0.2\times0.01=0.1\ \text{A m}^2\)
Step 2: \(\tau_{\max}=0.1\times0.2=0.02\ \text{N m}\)
Step 3: \(W=U(180^\circ)-U(0)=mB-(-mB)=2mB=0.04\ \text{J}\)
Worked derivation: \[W=\int_0^\pi mB\sin\theta\,d\theta=mB[-\cos\theta]_0^\pi=2mB\]
Check: \[\tau=0\text{ at }\theta=0\text{ (stable) and }180^\circ\text{ (unstable)}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{torque is greatest when the moment is perpendicular to the field, and the energy difference between aligned and anti-aligned is }2mB\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{omits }N\); (B) \(\text{work is not zero}\); (D) \(\text{torque is zero at }\theta=0\text{, and the work is }2mB\).
Key point: \(\tau=mB\sin\theta;\ W_{0\to\pi}=2mB\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating induced emf, current and total charge flow in a coil when the field through it changes, and why the charge is independent of the time taken
questions.question: A coil of \(200\) turns and area \(0.01\ \text{m}^2\) lies perpendicular to a field that falls uniformly from \(0.5\ \text{T}\) to \(0.1\ \text{T}\) in \(0.2\ \text{s}\). The coil's resistance is \(10\ \Omega\). What are the induced emf, current and total charge, and how does the charge change if the field falls in \(0.4\ \text{s}\) instead?
options: A) \(2\ \text{V},\ 0.2\ \text{A},\ 0.04\ \text{C}\); charge doubles
B) \(4\ \text{V},\ 0.4\ \text{A},\ 0.08\ \text{C}\); charge halves
C) \(0.02\ \text{V},\ 0.002\ \text{A},\ 0.0004\ \text{C}\); charge unchanged
D) \(\varepsilon=4\ \text{V},\ I=0.4\ \text{A},\ q=0.08\ \text{C}\); the charge is unchanged, because \(q=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}\) does not depend on the time taken
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(4\ \text{V},\ 0.4\ \text{A},\ 0.08\ \text{C}\); unchanged.
Given: \(N=200,\ A=0.01\ \text{m}^2,\ \Delta B=0.4\ \text{T},\ \Delta t=0.2\ \text{s},\ R=10\ \Omega\)
Formula/Principle: \(\varepsilon=N\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t};\ I=\dfrac\varepsilon R;\ q=I\Delta t=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}\)
Step 1: \(\varepsilon=\dfrac{200\times0.01\times0.4}{0.2}=4\ \text{V}\)
Step 2: \(I=\dfrac4{10}=0.4\ \text{A}\)
Step 3: \(q=0.4\times0.2=0.08\ \text{C}\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta t=0.4\ \text{s}:\ \varepsilon=2\ \text{V},\ I=0.2\ \text{A},\ q=0.2\times0.4=0.08\ \text{C}\]
Check: \[\frac{N\Delta\Phi}{R}=\frac{200\times0.004}{10}=0.08\ \text{C}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a slower change gives a smaller current for a longer time, so the product, the charge, stays the same}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{halves the emf; charge does not depend on time}\); (B) \(\text{charge does not halve}\); (C) \(\text{omits }N\text{ and the rate}\).
Key point: \(q=\dfrac{N\Delta\Phi}{R},\ \text{independent of }\Delta t\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Comparing resistors, inductors and capacitors in AC circuits — reactance versus frequency, phase of current, average power — and the effect of inserting an iron core into an inductor in series with a bulb
questions.question: How do a resistor, an ideal inductor and an ideal capacitor behave in an AC circuit, and what happens to a bulb in series with an inductor when a soft-iron core is inserted?
options: A) Inductive reactance falls with frequency and capacitive reactance rises; the bulb glows brighter
B) All three dissipate the same average power; the bulb is unaffected
C) The current leads the voltage in an inductor and lags it in a capacitor; the bulb brightens

D) \(R\) is independent of frequency with current in phase; \(X_L=\omega L\) rises with frequency and the current lags by \(\tfrac\pi2\); \(X_C=\tfrac1{\omega C}\) falls with frequency and the current leads by \(\tfrac\pi2\); average power is zero in ideal \(L\) and \(C\); the iron core increases \(L\) and hence \(X_L\), so the current falls and the bulb dims
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(R\) constant in phase; \(X_L\propto\omega\), lag; \(X_C\propto\tfrac1\omega\), lead; zero average power in \(L,C\); bulb dims.
Given: \(v=v_m\sin\omega t\)
Formula/Principle: \(X_L=\omega L;\ X_C=\dfrac1{\omega C};\ \bar P=V_{\text{rms}}I_{\text{rms}}\cos\phi\)
Step 1: \(\text{inductor: }\phi=\tfrac\pi2\ (\text{lag})\Rightarrow\cos\phi=0\Rightarrow\bar P=0\)
Step 2: \(\text{capacitor: }\phi=-\tfrac\pi2\ (\text{lead})\Rightarrow\bar P=0\)
Step 3: \(\text{iron core}:\ L\uparrow\Rightarrow Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}\uparrow\Rightarrow I\downarrow\)
Worked derivation: \[I_{\text{rms}}=\frac{V_{\text{rms}}}{\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L)^2}}\ \text{decreases as }L\text{ increases}\]
Check: \[\omega\to0:\ X_L\to0\ (\text{short}),\ X_C\to\infty\ (\text{open, blocks DC})\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the inductor opposes changes in current more strongly at higher frequency and with a larger inductance}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{frequency dependences reversed}\); (B) \(\text{ideal }L,C\text{ dissipate no average power}\); (C) \(\text{phases reversed}\).
Key point: \(X_L=\omega L\text{ (lag)},\ X_C=1/\omega C\text{ (lead)},\ \bar P=0\text{ in ideal }L,C\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating critical angles for glass, water and diamond against air and for a glass–water interface
questions.question: With refractive indices glass \(1.5\), water \(1.33\) and diamond \(2.42\), what are the critical angles for glass–air, water–air, diamond–air and glass–water?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(41.8^\circ,\ 48.8^\circ,\ 24.4^\circ,\ 62.5^\circ\).
Given: \(n_g=1.5,\ n_w=1.33,\ n_d=2.42\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sin C=\dfrac{n_{\text{rarer}}}{n_{\text{denser}}}\)
Step 1: \(\sin C_g=\dfrac1{1.5}=0.667\Rightarrow41.8^\circ;\ \sin C_w=\dfrac1{1.33}=0.752\Rightarrow48.8^\circ\)
Step 2: \(\sin C_d=\dfrac1{2.42}=0.413\Rightarrow24.4^\circ\)
Step 3: \(\sin C_{gw}=\dfrac{1.33}{1.5}=0.887\Rightarrow62.5^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[n\uparrow\Rightarrow\sin C\downarrow\Rightarrow C\downarrow:\ C_d<C_g<C_w\]
Check: \[\text{glass–water ratio near }1\Rightarrow C\text{ large}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the small critical angle of diamond traps light by repeated total internal reflection, giving its sparkle}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{glass and water swapped}\); (C) \(\text{uses complements}\); (D) \(\text{guessed values}\).
Key point: \(\sin C=n_2/n_1;\ \text{larger }n\Rightarrow\text{smaller }C\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Calculating fringe width in Young's double-slit experiment and its change when the apparatus is immersed in water or the slit separation is halved, and the appearance of white-light fringes
questions.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment, \(\lambda=600\ \text{nm},\ d=1.0\ \text{mm},\ D=1.0\ \text{m}\). What is the fringe width in air, in water (\(n=\tfrac43\)) and when \(d\) is halved in air, and what is seen with white light?
options: A) \(0.6\ \text{mm},\ 0.8\ \text{mm},\ 0.3\ \text{mm}\); all fringes white
B) \(6\ \text{mm},\ 4.5\ \text{mm},\ 12\ \text{mm}\); central fringe dark

C) \(\beta=0.6\ \text{mm}\), \(0.45\ \text{mm}\) in water, \(1.2\ \text{mm}\) with \(d\) halved; with white light the central fringe is white and nearby fringes are coloured, violet edges nearer the centre and red farther out
D) \(0.6\ \text{mm}\) in all cases
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(0.6,\ 0.45,\ 1.2\ \text{mm}\); white central fringe with coloured fringes.
Given: \(\lambda=6\times10^{-7}\ \text{m},\ d=10^{-3}\ \text{m},\ D=1\ \text{m}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\beta=\dfrac{\lambda D}{d};\ \lambda_{\text{medium}}=\dfrac\lambda n\)
Step 1: \(\beta=\dfrac{6\times10^{-7}\times1}{10^{-3}}=6\times10^{-4}\ \text{m}=0.6\ \text{mm}\)
Step 2: \(\beta_w=\dfrac{0.6}{4/3}=0.45\ \text{mm}\)
Step 3: \(d\to\tfrac d2\Rightarrow\beta=1.2\ \text{mm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\beta\propto\lambda\Rightarrow\beta_{\text{violet}}<\beta_{\text{red}};\ \text{at the centre path difference }=0\text{ for all colours}\Rightarrow\text{white}\]
Check: \[\text{units: }\frac{\text{m}\cdot\text{m}}{\text{m}}=\text{m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{wavelength shortens in water and fringe width varies inversely with slit separation}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{multiplies by }n\text{ and halves instead of doubling}\); (B) \(\text{factor of 10 error; central fringe is bright}\); (D) \(\beta\text{ depends on medium and }d\).
Key point: \(\beta=\lambda D/d;\ \text{in a medium }\beta/n\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
questions.sub_topic: Applying Einstein's photoelectric equation to find stopping potential, and the separate effects of intensity and frequency of the incident light
questions.question: A metal has work function \(2.0\ \text{eV}\). What is the stopping potential for \(3.0\ \text{eV}\) photons, what happens to it if the intensity is doubled, and what is it for \(4.0\ \text{eV}\) photons?
options: A) \(V_s=1.0\ \text{V}\); unchanged when intensity doubles (only the photocurrent doubles); \(2.0\ \text{V}\) for \(4.0\ \text{eV}\) photons
B) \(V_s=1.0\ \text{V}\); doubles to \(2.0\ \text{V}\) with double intensity; \(2.0\ \text{V}\)
C) \(V_s=3.0\ \text{V}\); unchanged; \(4.0\ \text{V}\)
D) \(V_s=5.0\ \text{V}\); halves; \(6.0\ \text{V}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(1.0\ \text{V}\); unchanged; \(2.0\ \text{V}\).
Given: \(\phi_0=2.0\ \text{eV};\ h\nu=3.0\text{ and }4.0\ \text{eV}\)
Formula/Principle: \(eV_s=K_{\max}=h\nu-\phi_0\)
Step 1: \(eV_s=3.0-2.0=1.0\ \text{eV}\Rightarrow V_s=1.0\ \text{V}\)
Step 2: \(\text{intensity}\uparrow\Rightarrow\text{more photons, same }h\nu\Rightarrow V_s\text{ unchanged, current}\uparrow\)
Step 3: \(eV_s=4.0-2.0=2.0\ \text{eV}\Rightarrow V_s=2.0\ \text{V}\)
Worked derivation: \[\nu_0=\frac{\phi_0}{h}=\frac{2.0\times1.6\times10^{-19}}{6.63\times10^{-34}}\approx4.8\times10^{14}\ \text{Hz}\]
Check: \[\frac{\Delta V_s}{\Delta(h\nu)}=\frac{1\ \text{V}}{1\ \text{eV}}=\frac1e\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{each electron absorbs one photon, so its maximum energy depends on photon energy, not on how many photons arrive}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{intensity does not change }V_s\); (C) \(\text{ignores the work function}\); (D) \(\text{adds the work function}\).
Key point: \(eV_s=h\nu-\phi_0;\ \text{intensity changes current only}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Using the mass-action law n_e n_h = n_i² to find the minority carrier density in a doped semiconductor and identifying its type
questions.question: Pure silicon has \(n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\ \text{m}^{-3}\). It is doped with \(10^{22}\ \text{m}^{-3}\) pentavalent donor atoms, all ionised. What are the hole density and the type of semiconductor?
options: A) \(n_h=2.25\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^{-3}\); n-type, with electrons \(\approx10^{22}\ \text{m}^{-3}\) as majority carriers
B) \(n_h=1.5\times10^{16}\ \text{m}^{-3}\); intrinsic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(n_h=2.25\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^{-3}\); n-type.
Given: \(n_i=1.5\times10^{16}\ \text{m}^{-3},\ N_D=10^{22}\ \text{m}^{-3}\)
Formula/Principle: \(n_en_h=n_i^2;\ n_e\approx N_D\ (N_D\gg n_i)\)
Step 1: \(n_e\approx10^{22}\ \text{m}^{-3}\)
Step 2: \(n_i^2=2.25\times10^{32}\ \text{m}^{-6}\)
Step 3: \(n_h=\dfrac{2.25\times10^{32}}{10^{22}}=2.25\times10^{10}\ \text{m}^{-3}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{n_e}{n_h}=\frac{10^{22}}{2.25\times10^{10}}\approx4.4\times10^{11}\]
Check: \[n_en_h=10^{22}\times2.25\times10^{10}=2.25\times10^{32}=n_i^2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{added electrons recombine with holes, so the hole density falls far below its intrinsic value}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{ignores doping}\); (C) \(\text{donors give n-type}\); (D) \(\text{divides }n_i\text{ by }N_D\text{ wrongly}\).
Key point: \(n_en_h=n_i^2;\ \text{donors}\Rightarrow\text{n-type}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Counting significant figures and applying the rules for addition, multiplication and rounding off
questions.question: Which set of significant-figure results is correct: the number of significant figures in \(0.007020\) and in \(4.700\times10^3\), the sum \(2.5+3.42+1.137\), the product \(3.0\times2.11\), and \(2.745\) and \(2.735\) rounded to three figures?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(4,\ 4;\ 7.1;\ 6.3;\ 2.74,\ 2.74\).
Given: \(0.007020,\ 4.700\times10^3,\ 2.5+3.42+1.137,\ 3.0\times2.11,\ 2.745,\ 2.735\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{leading zeros not significant; trailing zeros after the decimal point significant; sums: fewest decimal places; products: fewest significant figures; dropping a 5: leave an even preceding digit, raise an odd one}\)
Step 1: \(0.007020\to7,0,2,0\Rightarrow4;\ 4.700\times10^3\Rightarrow4\)
Step 2: \(2.5+3.42+1.137=7.057\to1\text{ decimal place}\Rightarrow7.1\)
Step 3: \(3.0\times2.11=6.33\to2\text{ s.f.}\Rightarrow6.3\)
Worked derivation: \[2.745:\ \text{preceding digit }4\text{ even}\Rightarrow2.74;\quad2.735:\ \text{preceding digit }3\text{ odd}\Rightarrow2.74\]
Check: \[\text{the result is no more precise than the least precise input}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{significant figures carry the precision of measurement; the even-digit rule avoids systematic upward bias in rounding}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{miscounts zeros; no rounding}\); (B) \(\text{counts leading zeros}\); (D) \(\text{wrong count and rounding}\).
Key point: \(\text{add: decimals; multiply: s.f.; trailing 5: round to even}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Distinguishing average and instantaneous velocity for non-uniform motion and obtaining instantaneous velocity as the limit of average velocity
questions.question: A particle moves along a line with \(x=5t^2\) (SI units). What is its average velocity over \(0\)–\(2\ \text{s}\), its instantaneous velocity at \(t=1\ \text{s}\), and its average velocity over \([1,1+\Delta t]\)?
options: B) \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\); \(10+5\Delta t\ \text{m s}^{-1}\), which tends to \(10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\) as \(\Delta t\to0\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) \(10;\ 10;\ 10+5\Delta t\to10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\).
Given: \(x=5t^2\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar v=\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t};\ v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\lim_{\Delta t\to0}\dfrac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}\)
Step 1: \(\bar v_{0\to2}=\dfrac{20-0}{2}=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(v=10t\Rightarrow v(1)=10\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)
Step 3: \(\bar v_{[1,1+\Delta t]}=\dfrac{5(1+\Delta t)^2-5}{\Delta t}=10+5\Delta t\)
Worked derivation: \[\lim_{\Delta t\to0}(10+5\Delta t)=10=v(1)\]
Check: \[\text{for uniform acceleration, }\bar v\text{ over }[0,2]=v\text{ at the midpoint }t=1\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{instantaneous velocity is the limit of average velocity over shrinking intervals}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }x(2)\text{ as velocity}\); (C) \(v(1)\ne20\); (D) \(\text{wrong expansion}\).
Key point: \(v=\lim\Delta x/\Delta t;\ \text{uniform }a:\ \bar v=v_{\text{mid-time}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Showing that static friction adjusts up to its limiting value, relating the angle of repose to μs, and comparing static, kinetic and rolling friction
questions.question: A \(5\ \text{kg}\) block rests on a horizontal floor with \(\mu_s=0.5\) (\(g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)). A horizontal push of \(10\ \text{N}\) is applied. What friction acts, what is the angle of repose for this pair of surfaces, and how do the friction types compare?
options: A) friction \(25\ \text{N}\), so the block moves backwards; angle of repose \(30^\circ\)
B) friction \(0\), since the block does not move; angle of repose \(60^\circ\)
C) friction \(10\ \text{N}\); angle of repose \(45^\circ\); rolling friction is the largest

D) static friction \(10\ \text{N}\), exactly balancing the push (limiting value \(\mu_sN=25\ \text{N}\) not reached); angle of repose \(\theta=\tan^{-1}\mu_s=\tan^{-1}0.5\approx26.6^\circ\); rolling friction \(<\) kinetic friction \(<\) limiting static friction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(10\ \text{N}\); \(\tan^{-1}0.5\approx26.6^\circ\); rolling \(<\) kinetic \(<\) limiting static.
Given: \(m=5\ \text{kg},\ \mu_s=0.5,\ F=10\ \text{N},\ g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(f_s\le\mu_sN;\ \text{angle of repose: }\tan\theta=\mu_s\)
Step 1: \(N=mg=50\ \text{N};\ f_{\max}=0.5\times50=25\ \text{N}\)
Step 2: \(F=10<25\Rightarrow\text{no motion}\Rightarrow f_s=10\ \text{N}\)
Step 3: \(\tan\theta=0.5\Rightarrow\theta\approx26.6^\circ\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{on the incline at repose: }mg\sin\theta=\mu_smg\cos\theta\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\mu_s\]
Check: \[\text{net horizontal force }=10-10=0\Rightarrow\text{block stays at rest}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{static friction is self-adjusting: it equals the applied force until the limiting value is reached}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{friction cannot exceed the applied force at rest}\); (B) \(\text{friction is not zero under a push}\); (C) \(\text{wrong angle; rolling friction is smallest}\).
Key point: \(f_s=F\text{ up to }\mu_sN;\ \tan\theta_{\text{repose}}=\mu_s\)
